item.content:encoded:
When I saw a tweet saying Hal Steinbrenner "shot a flamethrower" at Yankees captain Aaron Judge, I had my popcorn ready for the fireworks. I watched it once, then again, waiting for a shot that never came.
After the Rays swept the Yankees out of the ALDS, Judge said he was "hating every single moment" of the elimination and that the front office should go all-in and "do what they need to do" to fill the roster's holes. People heard a captain calling out his owner, but I heard a guy whose season had just ended, and not at all how he drew it up.
Why Hal Steinbrenner's Aaron Judge comments are a good sign for the Yankees
You have to remember what Judge's year looked like. A broken rib cost him more than three months, and a week after he returned, a calf strain put him right back on the injured list. When you're making $40 million a year and can't be on the field when your team needs you, it eats at you, and can take an emotional toll. His coaches and teammates know he wants to be out there, but it doesn't change the facts. I've sat in the clubhouse after a season ends, and I can promise you the first thought is not what they need to say to the media, and I think that's what a lot of people "felt" from Judge's comments.
Then, on Wednesday, Hal confirmed that a new deal for Brian Cashman is being worked out, and addressed Judge directly. He said he wasn't upset about the comments after the elimination game, that he had a "great conversation" with Judge the day before, and that with decisions coming after the World Series, Judge "is going to be a part of all that."
That's not a flamethrower. That's an owner who knows he has one of the greatest hitters ever for a limited window, and bringing the captain into roster conversations is how you protect a culture and redesign a winning one. Aaron Judge has earned every bit of that access.
He also said he has expectations of his players, mentioning the medical staff in the process, and (I think) some fans took that as the jab. I took it as the opposite. Judge set a standard after Game 3, and Hal agreed with him. An owner and a captain holding everyone to the same bar is exactly where you want this franchise, especially with so much uncertainty heading into this offseason's CBA.
Hal continued on and made sure to mention (maybe this is the jab?) that this team had the highest payroll in franchise history, and hasn't been shy about spending. Spending the most money and spending it on the right players aren't always the same thing, as plenty of expensive Yankees rosters have learned. Still, if I'm Judge, I'll take an owner who's happy to write the big check — now it's just about cashing it on the right guy.
Fans and media see a sound bite, while players see the relationship behind it, and those of us covering this team have a responsibility not to create a divide that isn't there. After a month of scorching takes about this core, it's easy to turn every quote into a feud. From the outside looking in, this looked like two people on the same page about running a business and competing for a championship together, and Yankees fans should take it as good news rather than another distraction.
If I'm Judge, I'm hanging up that phone call, then seeing the press conference and feeling like my owner has my back. Now the only question is whether the new ownership calculus turns that conversation into the pieces he asked for.

item.content:encoded:
In the hours, days and weeks since the Yankees’ latest postseason failure, their collective character has been dissected just as much as their disappointing play.
Does there need to be more public accountability going forward? Does a team with a reputation for getting sloppy in the summer and in October pay enough attention to details? Have manager Aaron Boone and captain Aaron Judge fostered a country club atmosphere? Is every player truly bothered each time the pinstripers get embarrassed in the playoffs? Are there enough killers, enough grinders, in the room?
Are the current Yankees living up to the franchise’s storied standards? Do they have a culture problem?
All of these talking points have been raised since the Rays swept the Yankees in the ALDS and extended the Bombers’ title drought to 17 seasons. Some are fair, some are over the top, but they’ve nonetheless been topics of discussion in print, over the airwaves, and on social media.
Shortly after the Yankees were knocked out of the playoffs, the Daily News asked a member of the organization what they made of all that talk, especially the public perception of some that players are not held accountable. The source, an everyday presence in the clubhouse and dugout, was granted anonymity so that they could speak freely.
“Not sure honestly,” they replied. “Feels like a band aid or an easy solution to a complex situation. Players don’t respond to that type of feedback. The best accountability is ownership. Everyone is responsible for the shared environment that is created. Do we need more collective ownership… maybe?”
But, they added, “Inserting a few more alphas who run around policing everyone isn’t as impactful as you’d think. That’s not the secret sauce.”
Asked how the Yankees could take more collective ownership if key personnel don’t change — Boone and general manager Brian Cashman have since been retained — the source went on to say, “Speaking generally here, if you’re not getting the result you desire, I usually turn to the process first. Process can always improve. It’s never complete.”
To be clear, the Yankees did not lose the ALDS because of culture. They lost because they couldn’t field in Game 2, and because their lineup, missing an injured Judge, couldn’t hit throughout the series. Hal Steinbrenner certainly harped on the latter, chastising his offense’s “detrimental” performance on Wednesday while issuing his annual October votes of confidence to Boone and Cashman.
But the aforementioned source isn’t the only person who has criticized, questioned or hinted at intangible issues since the Yankees’ season ended.
Joe Girardi, Boone’s predecessor and less of a players’ manager, wondered if anyone is addressing the blunders the Yankees seem to make too often on “The Show” podcast. CC Sabathia, who played with and for Boone, said current Yankees “don’t know what that standard is… because there’s no one in there keeping that standard,” and that franchise greats aren’t around enough to uphold that on the “All The Smoke” podcast. And Anthony Rizzo, who played for the Yankees as recently as 2024 and remains tight with Judge, said it’s “insanity” for the Yankees to “keep doing the same thing every year” when championships aren’t being won on his own pod.
Keep in mind, those three are no longer in the Yankees’ clubhouse every day. But Judge and Cam Schlittler are, and both talked about standards after the Yankees’ were toppled by Tampa.
“There’s a standard to winning a championship,” Judge said. “It’s black and white. There’s no gray area. It’s every day you show up to work. Every little thing you do is, ‘Are you working toward a championship or you’re not?’ So I think that’s the biggest thing, is just everybody in the room understanding you gotta bring it every single day, especially here in New York. There’s no days off, and it just comes down to the little things and just preparing every single day like you’re preparing for a championship game.”
Schlittler, the impending AL Cy Young and one of the Yankees’ certified killers, added, “All the pieces are there. The talent’s there. I think we got the best talent in the league. But at the end of the day, we didn’t meet the standard that we have as an organization. It’s the second year in a row we gotta go home thinking about that. We just gotta be better.”
Schlittler also said that “it didn’t seem like we really showed up today” after the Yankees made four errors and misplayed a few other balls in a humiliating Game 2 ALDS loss.
On Wednesday, Steinbrenner said that he found that comment “concerning,” and that he wanted to talk to Schlittler about it to get a fuller sense of what he meant. The owner also indicated that he would talk it over with Judge, who already discussed a number of issues with Steinbrenner on Tuesday after he insinuated that the Yankees have not been “all in” enough during his career.
Meanwhile, Cashman said that he has spoken to a few ex-Yankees since the season ended. While he declined to say who he talked to and didn’t want to detail what he called “healthy, diplomatic, professional” chats, the revelation came in response to a question about the various remarks made by Girardi, Sabathia and Rizzo.
“I run to problems if they’re problems that do exist,” Cashman said. “It’s kind of my nature. I kind of put the hard hat on, and if something is amiss, then I’m going to try to address it or determine whether that really is amiss or not, so I proactively made phone calls based on a lot of the commentary that’s been out there, and I’ll continue to do so.”
Cashman also said that those conversations yielded “some healthy pointers,” but that there is always “noise” in the New York market. He added that he and each person he hit up agreed that “those issues aren’t why we’re losing those games.”
But does Cashman, now preparing for his 30th season as GM, believe there needs to be a culture change?
“We’re always trying to push culture,” he said. “We’re always trying to find higher ground, and that’s why, again, if something raises up the flagpole of, ‘Hey, there might be something here,’ let’s talk about it. Let’s address it. The one thing I’m very proud about is that, right or wrong, this organization is progressive. We are open-minded.”
“We’re going to look into it,” Steinbrenner chimed in.
That said, neither Cashman, Steinbrenner nor Boone seemed to think that holding players accountable in public more often was a change worth pursuing.
Boone and players — who can hear his postgame comments in the clubhouse — insist that tough talks do happen behind the scenes. And Boone does occasionally let it be openly known when he’s unhappy with someone, like when Jazz Chisholm Jr. played second base with a lollipop in his mouth in June.
But the skipper’s typical unwillingness to call out players for mistakes — or even objectively analyze poor performances at times — in front of cameras has long been a source of fan frustration.
“There is probably a time and place for that,” Boone, preparing for his 10th season as manager, acknowledged. “But generally speaking, to me, that’s not leadership. That’s me giving red meat to people who want to be upset with somebody.
“To me, when we have issues as a club or with an individual player or with something that popped up within a game, I address those things. We address those things man-to-man. Sometimes if we have to address something within the group, we do that.”
Steinbrenner’s father, George, often used the public square to motivate his players during his reign as owner, but the new boss said that heavy-handed tactic was for a “different generation,” and certainly not his style.
“My dad and I are different in that respect. I’m not convinced it would be effective anyway,” Steinbrenner said, noting that he pops into the Yankees’ clubhouse once or twice a homestand. “It’s just not the way I’m going to operate. I’m going to talk to them face-to-face.”
Cashman concurred, stating that private settings are “more appropriate” and “the most professional way” to handle things. He also said that he feels “there’s a built-in accountability, to the extreme, that’s around us every day” because of the spotlight that shines on the Yankees.
As for some of the comments made by his former players, Boone wasn’t sure what Rizzo was specifically referring to, but he pushed back on Sabathia’s suggestion that ex-Yankees don’t hang around enough. Boone described special assistant and five-time World Series champ Andy Pettitte as “a big part of our staff,” and he is always inviting legends of yesteryear to spring training.
Boone also believes that the Yankees had “a lot of the right ingredients” this year. Rebuking the public discourse, he called the team’s clubhouse “an absolute strength for us.”
Cashman, meanwhile, disputed the notion that the Yankees are lacking competitive nature as they embark on another offseason that started too soon.
“I do think our players are prepared,” the GM said. “I do think they are wired the right way. They care.”

Yankees' Aaron Boone, Brian Cashman returns lead insider to admit 'change was necessary' appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees lost to the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS, marking another year under manager Aaron Boone and GM Brian Cashman in which the team failed to win a World Series. The team has not won the World Series since 2009 and, while they have made the playoffs in eight of nine seasons under Boone, they have been to just one World Series. Still, owner Hal Steinbrenner is backing Boone and Cashman, while blaming the players for the latest early exit.
Now, MLB insider Ken Rosenthal is saying maybe it was time for a change, speaking on Foul Territory.
"I understand the frustration of Yankees fans who are asking, 'What are we doing? Why are we doing this over and over again when it's the same ending every year?' Hal Steinbrenner, the owner, put it on the players, blaming the hitters yesterday. Well, who picks the hitters? That's Cashman. Who manages the hitters? That's Boone," Rosenthal said. "I don't know. I don't advocate, or I don't like to advocate for people getting fired, but in this particular case, it just seemed like change was necessary, and it sure seemed like at some point, you can't let the fans run the team, but their fans are so exasperated by what has happened in recent years, maybe their voice needs to be heard in a greater way than it has been."

With the lack of a World Series title this year, the Yankees have tied their longest streak between World Series wins. The Yankees went from 1979 through 1995 without a title, 17 seasons. The current streak is from 2010 through 2026, another 17 seasons. Now, fans are getting tired of the same thing every season. Steinbrenner still says his goal is a World Series, but his actions are saying something different.

Wednesday was an eventful day for the New York Yankees as Hal Steinbrenner and Brian Cashman sat before reporters (well, via Zoom, anyway), followed by Aaron Boone. The trio's press conferences brought plenty of revelations (including Cashman's new deal), as well as injury updates on key Yankees players Aaron Judge, Max Fried, and Giancarlo Stanton.
We'll start with Judge, who took a dig from Steinbrenner on Wednesday when the owner not-so-subtly suggested that his superstar slugger fell below the expectations of a dutiful employee at the end of the campaign. But anyway ... how's Judge's body (that kept him out of the postseason) feeling these days?
Aaron Judge scheduled for follow-up appointment regarding rib injury; expected to be ready for Spring Training
Cashman revealed that Judge has a follow-up appointment scheduled with Dr. Gregory Pearl to inspect the healing process of the rib injury that cost Judge the bulk of the 2026 regular season. Cashman reiterated his prior stance that Judge wasn't physically capable of competing in the postseason, while also asserting that the offseason should allow Judge to heal fully, rest, and be ready for 2027.
Max Fried won't need surgery to address bone bruises
According to Boone on Wednesday, no Yankees player is in need of surgery this offseason, including Judge and Fried, the latter of whom increasingly suffered from left elbow bone bruises in 2026. Fried recently had the elbow re-imaged (per Boone), and the ligament is apparently in a good place.
Fried did undergo Tommy John surgery back in 2014, which presented a reason to fear that his recurring elbow problem this season might lead to another going-under-the-knife. He spent two separate stints on the IL this season (in May and August) for the same bone bruise issue. But according to Boone, Fried is all in the clear heading into the winter!
Giancarlo Stanton is healthy, but his future Yankees role sounds uncertain
Of course Stanton is healthy now that the Yankees' season isn't happening! Stanton appeared in just 24 games out of 162 for the Yanks in the 2026 due to multiple calf ailments. He made a couple of cameos as a pinch hitter in the postseason but wasn't able to deliver (not an easy ask, given how much time he spent away from game action).
Beyond discussing Stanton's health status, Cashman also interestingly noted that the Yankees' designated hitter spot is up for grabs. It sounds like the Yankees have finally opened themselves up to the possibility that Stanton should be cast aside ... or at least not prioritized.
The 36-year-old slugger is entering the final guaranteed year of his contract in 2027. The Yankees figure to have something of a logjam at DH if Stanton remains healthy. Ben Rice, Luis García Jr. (provided he's still on the team), and Judge will all needs reps at DH next season.

New York Post | Grace McCarron: Hal Steinbrenner held court yesterday with members of the Yankee beat, albeit by Zoom which in and of itself is an interesting decision. The managing partner of the Yankees publicly backed GM Brian Cashman and manager Aaron Boone, proclaiming that both men did their jobs in the 2026 season and publicly announcing that Cashman's new contract is all but signed. Hal placed the blame for a disappointing season at the feet of the players on the roster, especially a "detrimental" offense.
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Continuing with the Steinbrenner Address, Hal was asked directly about comments made by current and former Yankees regarding the now-17 year World Series drought. In particular, he seemed to be a little chesty about Aaron Judge's remarks that the team hasn't gone "all in" and should, with George's son pointing to the richest payroll in franchise history as evidence of his commitment. If Judge was more of an extrovert he might point across boroughs to another team that spends like mad and doesn't have the results expected as an example that money misallocated is as bad as money unspent.
SNY | Danny Abriano: Finally, Mr. Steinbrenner set the table as one of the more powerful owners in baseball, admitting that he'd like to see a salary cap implemented in this round of CBA negotiations. It's the most important thing for the group of thirty monopolists, and it needs to be the most important thing for the union to remember too.
NBC Sports | Eric Samulski: We also got news that Aaron Judge's rib is still a bit of a question mark. The Yankee captain will have followup tests and surgery seems unnecessary, Brian Cashman telling us that he expects Judge to be ready in time for Spring Training, whenever that is.
FanGraphs | Ben Clemens: We get a final piece that's a little more pan-baseball, with the Fielding Bible Awards being announced today at 3 p.m. Eastern. item.content:encoded:
Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner blamed New York's players for the team's failure to win the World Series and defended manager Aaron Boone and general manager Brian Cashman, who is getting a new contract as he enters his 30th season in charge of baseball operations.
“I thought Boone managed a good season, especially with the pitching staff," Steinbrenner said Wednesday. "The bottom line is the players didn’t live up to their end of the bargain in the playoffs.”
New York has gone 17 seasons without a World Series title. That matches the Yankees' longest drought since winning their first championship in 1923, a gap between titles in 1978 and ’96.
“If we don’t win a championship while I’m here, I’m sure that will be a frontline story of it all and how people think of me and how a fanbase reacts,” Boone said. "I understand that.”
Steinbrenner spoke alongside Cashman during a joint Zoom news conference from team's spring training ballpark in Tampa, Florida, and Boone followed with a video news conference from Yankee Stadium.
New York went 93-68 and finished second in the AL East to Tampa Bay. After sweeping Boston 2-0 in an AL Wild Card Series, the Yankees were swept 3-0 by the Rays in a Division Series.
“In the end, the majority of the responsibility — I’ll say it for the fifth time — in my mind, my opinion, lies with the position players and the inability to score on a consistent basis throughout the course of the entire season for the most part,” Steinbrenner said. “Not on the shoulders of Aaron Boone does the blame lie.”
Captain Aaron Judge was limited to 66 games and hit .241 with 18 homers and 41 RBIs. The three-time AL MVP was sidelined from June 1 through Sept. 7 by a fractured rib, returned for seven games, then had a season-ending calf injury.
Giancarlo Stanton's regular season ended with a calf injury on April 24.
“Look, losing Stanton and losing Judge for 80-plus percent of the season in the offense’s defense was not part of the plan and it certainly had an effect," Steinbrenner said. “We just have to figure out how much of it was that.”
He doesn't feel a need to publicly pressure players in the manner of his father, George Steinbrenner.
“I'm not convinced that with this team, in this day and age, that that’s as big of a motivator as you think it is,” Hal Steinbrenner said. “Twenty, 25 years ago, different generation, just a different scenario.”
Boone heads into last season of contract
Boone finished his ninth season as manager and has one season left on a two-year contract extension agreed to in February 2025. The 53-year-old former third baseman has led New York to a 790-565 regular-season record and three first-place finishes in the AL East but a 27-30 postseason mark.
"At the end of the day, we haven’t won a championship with me at the helm," he said. "Ultimately that’s what has to happen to satisfy certainly myself — that's why I'm doing this — but to answer those questions ultimately.”
Steinbrenner and the Yankees front office evaluated Boone after the season-ending loss.
"We had a weeklong conversation about Aaron Boone and was he part of the problem this year, and I don’t believe he was. I think he had a good year managing-wise," Steinbrenner said. “But, yes, I would consider, of course, moving on from Aaron Boone if I thought he was a huge part of a problem.”
Boone defended not calling out players publicly for mistakes.
“I know I get accused sometimes of being too positive in the media and I would say if you watch my post(game) conferences this year, there were a lot of days where I was talking about our struggles. But does that mean I’m calling individuals out in a public way?” Boone said. "There is probably a time and place for that, but generally speaking to me that’s not leadership. That’s me giving red meat to people that want to be upset with somebody.”
Cashman will stay on as GM
Cashman, who turns 60 in July, said he and the team have agreed to a new contract and are working on minor details. He became general manager in February 1998 and is the most senior head of baseball operations in the major leagues — San Diego’s A.J. Preller, hired in August 2014, is second.
When Cashman took over from Bob Watson in 1998, it was the 15th change at GM since George Steinbrenner bought the Yankees in January 1973. Cashman has been the only GM under Hal Steinbrenner, who succeeded his father as controlling owner in November 2008.
New York has won four World Series, seven AL pennants and 15 AL East titles since Cashman became GM. He had been working under a four-year contract announced in December 2022.
“Cash is great every season,” Steinbrenner said. “The roster he put together, the team that we rolled out of spring training with was as good as any in baseball in my opinion. We had a lot of bumps and bruises along the way, but the team was fantastic and it was a world championship-caliber team.”
Financing with affiliat
e of Apollo Global Management
Yankee Global Enterprises, the team's parent company, announced a $2.6 billion financing agreement in August with Apollo Sports Capital, an affiliate of Apollo Global Management. The deal included debt and equity.
“It is not a precursor to fully selling the team,” Steinbrenner said. “The whole goal of the Apollo deal was to bring in capital into the company that would be there for us, to give us more financial stability for years and years to come, including the years when I’m out of here and the third generation is running the team.”

Shortly after the Yankees were swept by the Rays in the ALDS, Aaron Judge was asked how owner Hal Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman should react to the team’s latest postseason failure.
“We’re the Yankees,” said the back-to-back MVP, who was sidelined for the playoffs by a calf strain. “I feel like they should go all in and do what they need to do. If we got holes, it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you gotta go out there and get it. That’s why I signed back here to play with the Yankees, to fight for a championship every single year. We go all in. That’s what I do every offseason: get ready to give this team and the city everything I got. So I expect them to do the same.”
The captain’s response demanded a follow-up: does Judge feel the organization has gone all in enough during his 11-year, championship-less tenure?
“It’s tough to say,” Judge, 34, said after a long pause. “I want to trade for everybody and sign everybody every single year, but I know that’s not realistic. So they give us a winning team every single year, but that’s not good enough here in New York. We’re the Yankees. You gotta go out there and expect championships and go all in every year, so I’m excited to see what they do.”
On Wednesday, Steinbrenner addressed Judge’s pointed comments while conducting an autopsy of the Yankees’ shortcomings via Zoom. The owner said that he did not watch Judge’s full postgame interview after Game 3 of the ALDS, but a few of the slugger’s quotes were brought to his attention.
His reaction?
“Was I upset about it? No,” said Steinbrenner, who has a close relationship with Judge. “If I was a player, I would have expectations that my ownership group would do everything in their power every offseason to field a team that could win a championship. There’s nothing wrong with expectations. We did that this year. We had the highest payroll in the history of the organization. We got to a point later in the [last] offseason where we still felt we weren’t good enough, so we went out and signed [Cody] Bellinger to a huge contract. Glad we did. He’s a good player, so I definitely think we went all in this season. I definitely think we had a team that was every bit capable of winning a championship. No, it did not work out.
“And by the way, I have expectations of my players. I expect them to obey the rules, to work hard, to listen to their coaches and the trainers and the strength guys. Expectations are a good thing. Any relationship in life is a two-way street, and part of that is having expectations of each other. So no, I wasn’t bothered by it at all.”
As Steinbrenner alluded to, he financed a franchise record competitive balance tax payroll, projected to be $341.8 million, in 2026. That ranked third in baseball behind the Mets ($359.4 million) and Dodgers ($432.8 million), per Cot’s Contracts.
Judge, meanwhile, didn’t specify what he wanted the Yankees to do differently — or what he wants them to do going forward — after Game 3. He did, however, seem to take a shot at the Yankees’ so-called “run it back” approach — they retained a largely similar roster after getting bounced in the 2025 ALDS — despite endorsing the tactic in spring training and at the end of last year.
“The toughest thing is each year, besides us, every other team gets better,” Judge said. “Every other team’s adding new players, getting new coaches, new philosophies, things they can do to improve their team. So it’s not like, ‘Hey, we’re just going to run it back and we’ll be in the postseason.’”
While Judge didn’t vocalize his vision to reporters, Steinbrenner said that he and the right fielder had a “great conversation” on Tuesday that covered “a number of subjects.” The early offseason chats between owner and superstar have become an annual tradition, just like the Yankees’ premature playoff exits.
While Steinbrenner didn’t detail their most recent talk, he did say, “We’ve got some decisions that need to be made right after the World Series is over, essentially, and then some we have more time on. And [Judge is] going to be a part of all that. So, yeah, that’s the deal.”
Steinbrenner, speaking for himself, did take exception to the Yankees’ inconsistent offense this season, which he called “detrimental.” Of course, Judge’s injuries played a part in the lackluster performance, as he missed 99 days with a fractured rib and then the playoffs with his calf strain. But Steinbrenner believes the Yankees had enough talent to cover for Judge’s absences — Bellinger, Trent Grisham and Giancarlo Stanton also missed significant time — and so the club is going to look at potential changes to its coaching staff and hitting philosophies.
Some lineup turnover is also expected with Grisham and Jazz Chisholm Jr. headed for free agency.
“As a whole, they were very inconsistent when it came to run scoring,” Steinbrenner said, “and they were inconsistent for long periods of time.”
As for Judge’s injuries, those also became a point of contention between the player and the organization this year.
He repeatedly pushed to skip a rehab assignment when he returned from his rib injury and got his wish, but he only lasted seven games before suffering a moderate calf strain. Judge then seemed to take issue when Aaron Boone revealed the severity of his strain, and he said he wanted to make what would have been an expedited return for the Wild Card Series and ALDS.
Judge was left off both rosters. On Wednesday, Cashman said that there were no regrets on the Yankees’ end, as “he just wasn’t physically able to post for us” due to the calf strain.
Cashman, also on Wednesday’s Zoom, added that Judge underwent an end-of-season physical and that his rib “came out fine.” Judge has a follow-up scheduled with a specialist, Dr. Gregory Pearl, but the Yankees believe he’s in a strong spot health-wise.
“As of right now, we feel like we’re in a good place,” Cashman said, “and he can take advantage of the rest of the winter and be ready to go when spring training starts.”

A possible lockout may alter New York's plans. Without a salary cap, the Yankees are usually one of the top spending organizations in the Majors.
That might not be enough to appease Judge. Perhaps the Yankees are making the wrong decisions when it comes to roster construction.
Spending money is great, but it won't matter if the players on the field don't make sense as a unit.
"Externally, the Yankees have a great one-two punch in their starting rotation with Cam Schlittler and Max Fried, but adding another ace wouldn't hurt," Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller wrote. "Also, adding a right-handed corner infielder to pair with Luis Garcia Jr. and Ryan McMahon would make a lot of sense."
Of course, the Yankees have major decisions to make with impending free agents, including Jazz Chisholm Jr. and David Bednar. How will they handle the rest of Giancarlo Stanton's contract?
Almost 35, the clock is ticking for Judge to win a World Series before his career comes to an end.
Now more than ever, the Yankees must be aggressive in their pursuit of top free agents and make smart decisions in the trade market.

Boone's consistent success in the regular season has been overshadowed by his inability to lead New York to its first World Series championship since 2009.
Steinbrenner spoke to the media on Wednesday to explain his thought process, and the owner ended up putting more blame on the players than the manager or the front office. item.content:encoded:
Two weeks after their playoff elimination in Game 3 of the ALDS, New York Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman held a postmortem press conference on Wednesday. Steinbrenner called the team's season a "failure" and blamed the offense for the quick postseason exit. The Yankees scored five runs in the three-game sweep against the Tampa Bay Rays.
"I have never suggested that a season like this season is a success," Steinbrenner said. "I am often asked, 'Was the entire season a failure?' Winning 93 games is not a failure. Playing in the Division Series is not a failure. It became a failure because we did not do well. I don't believe I've ever called a season that we didn't win a world championship successful."
New York's offense went in the tank after captain Aaron Judge was placed on the injured list with a rib fracture in early June. Judge's last game before going on the shelf was May 31, which was effectively the end of his season. He returned in September, played seven games, then suffered a calf strain that sidelined him the rest of the year. Judge did not play in the postseason.
"The players didn't live up to their end of the bargain in the playoffs," Steinbrenner added. "... We're going to look at everything (this offseason). I was disappointed with the offense. They were inconsistent for long periods of time."

|---|---|---|
| Plate appearances | 2,222 | 3,775 |
| Runs per game | 5.17 (4th in MLB) | 4.25 (23rd in MLB) |
| Homers per game | 1.46 (1st) | 1.34 (5th) |
| Batting average | .243 (13th) | .230 (29th) |
| On-base percentage | .334 (5th) | .297 (30th) |
| Slugging percentage | .436 (2nd) | .394 (23rd) |
No decisions regarding the future of the coaching staff, including hitting coach James Rowson, have been made yet, and neither Cashman nor Steinbrenner would get into offseason roster-building strategies. The Yankees have one of the game's best pitching staffs, but the offense was lacking, and Judge's absence was only part of that. As good as he is, he is just one player.
"Do I like sitting here trying to explain why? No, but I am going to analyze, in a very objective way, what we think went wrong," Steinbrenner said about falling short of the World Series again. "... I'm upset sitting here and having to answer these questions. Absolutely, and I know how upset our fans are, but believe me, we're going to be doing everything we can."
The Yankees have not won the World Series since 2009 and their 17-year championship drought is tied with 1979-95 for the longest in franchise history. Here now is what you need to know about Cashman's and Steinbrenner's postmortem press conference.
Cashman will return
As expected, Cashman will return for what will be his 30th season as general manager in 2027. Cashman's contract was set to expire this offseason, but he confirmed the two sides have agreed to a new deal, and they just need to finalize details before putting pen to paper. "We're locked and loaded," Cashman said about his contract status.
"Cash is great every season," Steinbrenner said. "I mean, I think the roster he put together, the team that we rolled out of spring training with, was as good as any in baseball, in my opinion."
The Yankees have not had a losing season during Cashman's tenure and they've made the postseason nine times in the last 10 seasons. At the same time, they've won three division titles in the last 14 seasons, and the World Series drought is tied for the longest in franchise history. Cashman's recent teams win a lot during the regular season and not much in October.
"The first step of the process is making sure you can punch a ticket and get there," Cashman said about the team's postseason failures. "Then, everything is reset. You need to have as many talented players as you possibly can on both sides of the ball."
Boone will return as well
and Steinbrenner said there was a "weeklong conversation" about Boone's future and whether he should return. Next year is the final season on Boone's contract and there have not been any talks about a contract extension. He will manage next year as a lame duck.
"The inability to score on a consistent basis throughout the course of the entire season, not on the shoulders of Aaron Boone," Steinbrenner said. "... Talking about this season, I thought Boone managed a good season, especially with the pitching staff. We had a lot of additions and subtractions in the rotation throughout the course of the season. Our bullpen was absolutely exhausted by the end of the season. He got through all that and he got us to the playoffs."
Boone also spoke Wednesday and said he's "very comfortable" managing next season without a contract extension. He also acknowledged that the Yankees have consistently lost to higher-seeded teams in the postseason during his tenure. The Yankees are 7-0 in postseason series against teams with a worse regular-season record, and 1-8 against teams with a better record.
"At the end of the day, we haven't won a championship with me at the helm," Boone said. "That's what has to happen to satisfy myself and to answer those questions [about being the right person for the job] ultimately."
Reaction to Judge's comments
Following the team's ALDS elimination, Judge pushed for the Yankees to go "all-in" this offseason. "We're the Yankees. I feel like they should go all-in and do what they need to do. And if we got holes, it's finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, we got to go out there and get it," . Steinbrenner was asked for his reaction to those comments.
"Was I upset about it? No," Steinbrenner said. "If I was a player, I would have expectations that my ownership group would do everything in their power every offseason to win a championship. We did that this year. We had the highest payroll in the history of the organization. I definitely think we went all-in this season. We had a team that was every bit capable of winning a championship. No, it did not work out. I have expectations of my players. I expect them to obey the rules, work hard, listen to their coaches, trainers, strength guys. Expectations are a good thing."
As for Judge's health, he will see a specialist for one more evaluation of his rib, but otherwise is in a good spot. "We feel like we're in a good place. He can take advantage of the rest of the winter and be ready to go when spring training starts," Cashman said.
Steinbrenner declined to discuss CBA talks
Steinbrenner is on MLB's labor committee and thus at the forefront of the owners' push for a salary cap. He has said in the past that he supports a salary cap as long as it comes with a salary floor, though he declined to answer labor questions on Wednesday, including questions about why he would support a salary cap that would limit his team's ability to leverage its financial might.
"Listen, guys, we're two days away from the World Series. This, in my mind, is a time to celebrate the game. Now's not the time I'm going to start labor conversations. It just is not," Steinbrenner said. "... I helped craft the proposals that we have given at the bargaining table and I support those proposals in their entirety. That should answer your question."
The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 and, barring a surprise agreement between MLB and the MLBPA, the owners are expected to lock out the players at that time.

New York Yankees chairman Hal Steinbrenner directed blame toward players, not general manager Brian Cashman or manager Aaron Boone, for his club's ALDS elimination.
Steinbrenner expressed faith in Boone in a Wednesday press conference during which he confirmed an upcoming extension for Cashman.
"I thought Boone managed a good season, especially with the pitching staff," Steinbrenner said (h/t SNY Yankees).
Steinbrenner continued, "He got us to the playoffs, and the bottom line is, the players didn't live up to their end of the bargain in the playoffs."
The Yankees were eliminated from the postseason Oct. 7 after getting swept from the divisional series by the Tampa Bay Rays.
The run marked the club's second consecutive ALDS elimination, and the third straight season during which the Yankees have won more than 90 games but fallen short of a title.
Steinbrenner said Wednesday he felt the blame for that early exit could be directed toward an offense that batted a combined .130 with a dozen hits and five total runs in three games against the Rays.
"I don't think you can pin the season, and the unacceptable end to it, on Aaron," Steinbrenner said. "I don't think you can pit it on [Cashman] based on the roster he put together.
"Again, the offense, not the pitching but the offense, had a big part, in my opinion, of why we didn't get— and I don't mind saying it— where we strive to get every year."
Steinbrenner concluded, "I absolutely believe we had a team that was capable of winning a championship."
Cashman, who has served as general manager of the Yankees since 1998, said Wednesday he was finalizing an extension with the club.
Steinbrenner said as of Wednesday he had not discussed a similar contract with Boone, although the Yankees had held an internal "weeklong conversation" about the managerial position.
He added he did not see Boone as "a huge part of the problem" and was willing to consider an extension going forward.
Boone is currently heading into the final season of his contract in 2027, per MLB.com's Brent Maguire.
Steinbrenner concluded he ultimately refused to look at the season as "a complete failure" despite not returning to the World Series, in which the Yankees last competed in 2024 before suffering elimination at the hands of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
"Winning 93 games is not a failure. Playing in the division series is not a failure," Steinbrenner said. "It became a failure because we did not do well."
The Yankees still succeeded in attracting fans last season despite the club's continued lack of postseason success. Listed in March as the most lucrative team in baseball with an $8.5 billion valuation by Forbes, the Yankees ranked second only to the Dodgers in average attendance this season by drawing crowds of more than 41,700 to the Bronx.
Steinbrenner named Ben Rice as a "bright spot" but said he would overall be looking at his offense from "top to bottom."
"This has been twice, now, where the offense just hasn't lived up to their end of the bargain," Steinbrenner said.
Those comments could potentially offer some insight into how Cashman plans to approach the 10 players he has hitting free agency after this disappointing end to the 2026 season.
It seems likely the Yankees could prioritize retaining pitcher David Bednar over players like Trent Grisham and Jazz Chisholm, who could potentially be walking should the Yankees look to overhaul their offense this winter.

The New York Yankees on October 19 confirmed something baseball fans everywhere expected. Aaron Boone will return as the Yankees' manager in 2027. Many Yankees fans are unimpressed with the decision, which means Boston Red Sox fans are celebrating it.
If Boone was going to be fired, it probably would've happened shortly after the Tampa Bay Rays' ALDS sweep of New York. Though, Boone actually managed the series quite well, and there isn't much he could've done about the Yankees' .431 team OPS and .125 batting average with runners in scoring position.
Boone has been the skipper in the Bronx since 2018. They've made the playoffs in all but one season since then, made the World Series once but have no titles to show for their efforts. For the "27 rings" Yankees, that's a long drought. Though it wasn't started by Boone, his past managerial efforts haven't helped.
The 2027 season is the final one on Boone's contract. The Yankees haven't offered him an extension, so they could be ready to move on next year. They might be wise to hold onto Boone — the manager options available this year aren't the most inspiring, and some reporters, including Jon Heyman of the New York Post, believe that New York could be the next team to hire Alex Cora. The longtime Red Sox manager is taking the 2027 season off and the Yankees could be waiting out Boone's contract to land a highly coveted skipper next year, which would be a gut punch to Sox fans.

As Yankees fans debated the degree of fault than can be placed on Boone for the team's playoff struggles in recent years, former Yankees players have taken the conversation in a different direction. They've largely had nothing but praise for Boone, but critiqued the larger culture of the organization.
CC Sabathia has said the Yankees' "standard" hasn't been upheld — whatever that means. Nick Swisher believes the players in the locker room need to take accountability, form a bond and get it together. Alex Rodriguez said the front office needs a "philosophy change." Even David Ortiz has made comments about the degradation of the Yankees' culture and attitude from the late 90s and early 2000s. Yet, none of the issues are Boone's fault (at least, not his alone) and he's been a great manager in their eyes.
Regardless of what's wrong with the Yankees and who's to blame for their mediocrity, Red Sox fans are happy they're seemingly uninterested in figuring it out. Boone and Brian Cashman remain for at least one more season and that probably means New York's season will end the way it always has under their watch — without a title.

The New York Yankees need some type of shakeup after getting swept in the ALDS by the AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays. The likelihood is that GM Brian Cashman and manager Aaron Boone aren't going anywhere. But the Yankees shouldn't just run back the same roster and hope Aaron Judge stays healthy in 2027. They should operate like the Yankees of old, where they were stacking their team every year and going hard for a World Series title.
As a result of a weak free agency class on the offensive side, the Yankees should explore the trade market in order to upgrade their lineup. They could look to the Houston Astros, who have some attractive trade pieces in their infield. For that, we're going to look at two Astros the Yankees should target via trade and one they should stay away from.
A trade the Yankees must make with the Houston Astros
Astros shortstop Jeremy Pena could be on his way out of Houston after the two sides failed to reach an agreement on a contract extension. Pena will be a free agent after next season and the Astros should trade him if they aren't going to retain the homegrown shortstop.
The Yankees are the perfect fit for Pena, who would instantly boost their offense. A trade for Pena would probably start with George Lombard Jr. However, the Yankees have the money to keep Pena for the long-term, and a lineup centered around Judge, Pena, Ben Rice, Cody Bellinger and Luis Garcia Jr. could contend for a World Series title. Pena, if available, should be the Yankees' top trade target this offseason.
A Yankees fallback option
If the Yankees can't land Pena, they should pivot to Astros third baseman Isaac Paredes. The Yankees have a major hole at third base and the position has been an issue for several years. Paredes has a $13.35 million club option for 2027, which Houston will likely pick up. That salary amount is more than affordable for a trade partner to take on, including the Yankees. Paredes is coming off a big season, where he hit 25 home runs, drove in 94 RBI, had an .806 OPS and posted a 4.0 bWAR in 155 games. The Yankees shouldn't give up a Lombard or Spencer Jones for Paredes, but they have other pieces that could get a deal done, specifically their young pitching depth. Even one season of Paredes would be a significant upgrade over Ryan McMahon at third base.
An Astros trade target the Yankees should stay far away from
First baseman Christian Walker is another infielder the Astros could trade in the offseason. Walker has one more year on his deal for $20 million in 2027, and Houston's new GM could look to shed that salary. Walker was once viewed as a fit for the Yankees in recent years, but that's no longer the case. The first baseman is turning 36 years old next season and comes along with an expensive price tag for a player, who has posted a sub-.300 on-base percentage and combined 2.3 bWAR across the past two seasons. Walker does have power at the plate and brings strong defense at the first base position. That being said, the Yankees already have Garcia and Rice to man first base. Acquiring Walker at this point in time wouldn't make much sense for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
Shortly after the New York Yankees were eliminated from the playoffs by the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Divisional Series round of the postseason tournament, it was reported that Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner had decided to retain team senior vice president/general manager Brian Cashman and manager Aaron Boone.
Monday reports confirmed that Boone, who is signed through the 2027 campaign, will remain the Yankees' skipper through the uncertain MLB offseason. Jon Heyman of the New York Post later noted that "it’s surely only a matter of time before we hear" that Cashman has inked a new deal with the Yankees.
For a piece published on Tuesday, Bob Klapisch of NJ Advance Media explained why Steinbrenner signed off on moves that are unpopular among pockets of Yankees fans.
"The coming labor dispute, which could be the longest and most contentious in the sport's history, is a factor in Steinbrenner's thinking," Klapisch wrote. "The season's start will almost certainly be delayed. The question is how long the owners and the [MLB Players Association] will hold out on the salary cap issue. The worst scenario says it'll be July — or just around the All-Star break — before both parties decide they've suffered enough. But that would leave a new Yankees manager in limbo for nearly nine months. Under MLB rules, a lockout halts all business and communication between team personnel — including managers, coaches, executives, and medical/training staff — and players covered by the lockout. It would be unfair, not to mention impractical, for Boone's potential replacement to hastily pull together the moving parts after a settlement."
While Boone is popular among key Yankees players such as slugger and team captain Aaron Judge, members of the franchise's fan base have spent years campaigning for Steinbrenner to make a change. Boone failed to guide the Yankees to a single World Series appearance from 2018 through the 2023 season. The Los Angeles Dodgers then needed just five games to bounce Boone's Yankees from the 2024 World Series, and the Bronx Bombers have since come up short of trips to the AL Championship Series in back-to-back years.
"October is all that matters," Klapisch added about Boone's future with the Yankees. "This was the verdict: The Yankees were booed off the field after the season-ending Game 3 loss to the Rays. Chants of 'Fire Boone!' thundered throughout the Stadium. The atmosphere has never been this hostile towards the manager. It's unlikely the anti-Boone fever will cool over the next few months. The movement will be dormant, but a new season — whenever it begins — will bring fresh calls for change."
Judge has challenged Steinbrenner and Cashman to "go all-in and do what they need to do" this offseason to give Boone a roster capable of winning the World Series. While it's unclear what such moves may look like before the expected work stoppage begins in early December, it sounds like Boone may have to guide the 2027 Yankees beyond the ALCS to remain the club's manager through the start of the 2028 campaign.

Aaron Boone will return as manager of the New York Yankees in 2027, the Bergen Record reports. Next season is the final season on Boone's contract and will be his 10th season as Yankees manager. New York is 790-565 (.583) in nine seasons under Boone. The Yankees have reached the postseason eight times in those nine seasons but have not won the World Series.
"That's for another day," Boone said when asked about his job status after the Yankees were swept by the AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS. "Right now is about trying to reflect on this, trying to connect with guys right now as much as I can. Appreciative of a lot of things, but those conversations and things are for another day."
Unless the Yankees give Boone a contract extension, he will enter next season as a lame duck, and that season could come with a World Series or bust mandate. The Yankees have had only three managers in the last 30 years: Joe Torre from 1996-2007, Joe Girardi from 2008-17, and Boone since 2018. Torre and Girardi both won the World Series within their first two seasons.
Why the Yankees are sticking with Boone
The Yankees have not fired a manager who was under contract since Stump Merrill after the 1991 season (Torre and Girardi were let go after their contracts expired). Hal Steinbrenner is much more patient than his father, perhaps to his detriment, but Steinbrenner and GM Brian Cashman are supportive of Boone. That all made Boone's return more likely than not.
Furthermore, this is a bad offseason to need a new manager. Team personnel, including managers, can not communicate with players during a lockout, which is considered likely when the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. Relationship-building with players is most of the job, and it will be difficult for a new manager to foster those during the lockout.
Only the Los Angeles Dodgers have won more games than the Yankees since Boone was named manager in 2018. This is a franchise that is judged on championships, however, and New York has not won a World Series since 2009. The Yankees have won just one pennant since then (2024), and their 17-year title drought is tied for the longest in franchise history with their 1979-95 stretch.

The New York Yankees are sticking with Aaron Boone next season after all.
After speculation that the team would move on following their latest postseason exit, Boone will return as the Yankees manager in 2027, according to USA Today's Pete Caldera and the YES Network's Jack Curry.
Boone signed a two-year extension through the 2027 MLB season in Feb. 2025, months after the Yankees lost the World Series to the Los Angeles Dodgers. After two straight eliminations in the ALDS, many expected his time would be up in New York after nine seasons. Instead, Boone will now manage through the end of his current deal.
The 2026 season saw the Yankees finish second in the AL East for the second straight season and win 90 games for the seventh time over a full season under Boone. It's been the postseason where the Yankees fell short more often than not under the 53-year-old.

The Yankees hold a 27-30 playoff record under Boone, which included three trips to the ALCS and one World Series appearance. His teams were 18-5 as the higher seed in a series and 9-25 as the lower seed. The Yankees were the No. 4 seed in 2026 and beat the No. 5 seed Boston Red Sox in the wild-card round before being swept by the top-seeded Tampa Rays in the ALDS.
Without Aaron Judge and with Giancarlo Stanton only available as a pinch-hitter, the Yankees batted .130 in the ALDS, and three of their five RBI came from Ben Rice. Their pitching was what kept them in games, as evidenced by a 1.88 team ERA, 0.81 team WHIP and a .173 opponent batting average.
Other teams picked up on the weaknesses of Boone's Yankee teams. The Dodgers told their players their 2024 World Series opponents were "talent over fundamentals" and were bound to self-destruct. Toronto Blue Jays announcer Buck Martinez labeled the AL East rivals as "not a good team" last season, saying they were mistake-prone in the field and on the bases.
Those criticisms were only hardened after seeing Austin Wells' baserunner mistake in Game 1 against the Rays and then the Yankees' defensive breakdown in Game 2.
General manager Brian Cashman has been in charge for 29 seasons. Boone is just the third manager to work under him. The Yankees last won the World Series in 2009 and are in the midst of a 17-year championship drought. The boos heard after Trent Grisham's series-ending strikeout against the Rays showed how frustrated the fanbase is with the team's current state.
But regardless of their feelings, Cashman isn't ready to hire a new manager just yet. It's unclear what changes he will make this winter, if any major ones at all, in hopes of returning the franchise to contender status.

item.content:encoded:
We're not quite at the point in the year where the rumor mill is churning in full force, making this current wave of New York Yankees rumors something of an appetizer and a sign that things are going to get much crazier very soon. The looming lockout sets a transaction deadline of December 1, unless the league and the players' union miraculously come to an agreement before then.
That means the month of November is going to be fast and furious. We've already heard about the Yankees' supposed interest in trading for Xavier Edwards, as well as a possible connection to Randy Arozarena. Now, we've got a stack of more fresh rumors to sort through.
Yankees are expected to shop Luis Gil ahead of the November 20 non-tender deadline
It's amazing how far Luis Gil has fallen. The 28-year-old went from 2024 AL Rookie of the Year to a potential centerpiece of a Kyle Tucker trade ahead of the 2025 season to a guy on the roster bubble.
Now, according to Joel Sherman of the New York Post, New York is expected to explore trading Gil before the November 20 non-tender deadline. At this point, he's a reclamation project who, at best, could fetch a change-of-scenery candidate or a lottery-ticket-type prospect or two.
"Keep in mind, Gil and [Clarke Schmidt] are guys, they do not have minor league options left," Sherman explained. "So, they're either on the team next year, or they have to go through waivers. So, if the Yankees feel like they can't help in the rotation, they can't help in the bullpen, there's going to be a thought about either non-tendering or trying to trade one or both."
Sounds like Schmidt is very much in the same boat as Gil, though his recent injury woes might make him even more likely to be non-tendered.
A pair of bullpen arms appear to be in the Yankees' crosshairs on the trade market
After making mostly addition-by-subtraction moves to the bullpen last offseason and failing to address it aside from trading away Camilo Doval at the trade deadline, it sounds like maybe, just maybe, Brian Cashman is going to get serious about revitalizing the relief corps.
On a recent episode of the Pinstripe Post Podcast, Sherman revealed a pair of reliever trade targets that he says the Yankees have liked for a long time, right-handers Jeremiah Estrada and Anthony Bender.
Estrada of the San Diego Padres is a high-octane arm with a big strikeout rate, though he's not without concerns. The 28-year-old hit the IL thrice in 2026, starting with right elbow tendonitis in April, followed by right knee inflammation in June, and finally a right shoulder impingement ended his season early on August 26. His average fastball velocity fell to 95.8 miles per hour this year from 97.9 miles per hour in 2025, and while he struck out 30.2% of batters he faced, he also issued walks at a 12.7% clip.
Marlins reliever Anthony Bender has been someone who has been linked to the Yankees before. He'd also add a much-needed strikeout punch to the 'pen, but in a different way. The 31-year-old is very much an East-West pitcher, with his slider dominating his pitch usage coming in at 65% this year. He pairs that with a sinker that he goes to 32% of the time. Bender's season was impacted for a second straight year with a right shin stress reaction. He tossed 34 1/3 innings in 2026, posting a 2.62 ERA with a 29.3% strikeout rate and an 8.6% walk rate.
It should be noted that Estrada is controllable through the 2029 season, while Bender hits free agency at the end of next season.
Yankees could eye a potential center field platoon partner for Spencer Jones
Lastly, Sherman reported that the Yankees have had past interest in Washington Nationals center fielder Jacob Young, and thinks that they could revisit a trade for the 27-year-old again this offseason to partner with, or even ensure against, Spencer Jones and possible regression.
Young is a glove-first, right-handed hitting outfielder with speed. His bat is very much a work in progress, with him posting a .648 OPS in 2024 and a .583 OPS in 2025 before turning in a career-best .707 performance in 2026. The biggest development in his offensive game has been his ability to hit lefties, slashing .282/.353/.423 against southpaws this year.
It's an interesting fit because, despite being a left-handed hitter, Jones performance against left-handed pitching was one of his biggest strengths. There are questions about his defense, though, and Young would be a nice hedge there. Young also feels like a Yankees kind of player in the Harrison Bader mold.
He has three years of team control remaining, meaning he won't come cheap, especially since his skill set and position could have some viewing him as a starting-caliber player rather than a fourth outfielder. This could make sense, but it all depends on cost.

The New York Yankees' 2026 season ended in familiar fashion, with the Yanks vanquishing the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series and then getting completely dominated in the ALCS by a separate AL East rival.
It was the Tampa Bay Rays this year who embarrassed Aaron Boone's club (slightly different from last year's ALDS loss to the Toronto Blue Jays), and Boone's taken plenty of flak from the fanbase and media in the days since the Yankees' season officially ended. So has GM Brian Cashman.
What's made the buzz all the more ominous is that neither Boone nor Cashman have appeared for the customary end-of-season press conference. Fans are wondering what's taking so long.
Why haven't the Yankees held or even announced an end-of-season presser?
Last season, the Yankees allowed eight days to elapse between their elimination at the hands of the Jays (on October 8) and their end-of-season presser (October 16). On an identical schedule, this would have Cashman and Boone "due" to appear before the media at any moment, seeing as the Yanks were booted out of the playoffs this time around on October 7. But we haven't heard a peep from the organization about when the presser's going to take place. All we have so far is Bob Klapisch saying "the silence will likely be broken next week". Odd.
So, for now, we'll have to bank on comments from both Boone and Cashman that were made during the final hours of the season. Speaking after Game 3, Boone described the Yankees' clubhouse as "broken" and said that conversations about his job security were "for another day" while indicating that he expects to return in 2027. Cashman, whose contract is up, called Boone a "really good manager" before Game 3.
We also heard from Yankees captain Aaron Judge shortly after his team was bounced. Judge backed Boone publicly (but does he actually feel this way?) and vaguely suggested that the front office should go all in this offseason (nothing resembling a demand that would've pleased many fans).
So, yes ... we've heard from individuals, but there hasn't been the collective presser from the Boone/Cashman brain trust that everyone's anticipating. Surely, once the press conference does happen, both men will be asked once again to explain the decision to keep Judge and his ailing calf on ice throughout the postseason.
But there are far more ominous questions swirling around the Yankees, especially concerning Boone's future. Plenty of analysts (Buster Olney among them) assume the Yankees will stick with Boone for at least one more season. This makes some sense, especially given a possible lockout. Transitioning to a new leader during a time filled with many unknowns might be an unwise move.
Are the Yankees delaying their end-of-year press conference due to Aaron Boone?
The Boone situation is a complicated one. He did a great job this regular season (perhaps his best season as Yankees manager!), considering all of the injuries the Yankees suffered, most of all Judge's missed time. But another playoff failure was simply too much for many fans and former players to swallow. There's a growing narrative that change is needed. The "Yankee Standard" has been lost and must be found. Why should Boone be tasked with finding it? On the other hand, if not Boone, who?
Stability isn't the issue here. The Yankees are incredibly consistent and have been under the Cashman/Boone regime. It's just that they are consistently good, not great. And that's not what Yankees culture is actually about, historically. It's about championships, and nothing less. The mindset of George Steinbrenner no longer rules over this franchise, and it all feels very un-Yankee-like.
Understandably, continued silence from the organization about the end-of-season presser has fans' imaginations on fire. Is Hal Steinbrenner contemplating firing Boone? And what of Cashman's fate? The longer we don't hear anything, the weirder and wilder the fan fictions and made-up explanations will become. At this point, it behooves the Yankees to just come out and make an announcement, even if it's just to say that the presser's being delayed.

Some would say that 2026 was a tumultuous season for the Yankees’ skipper, and there is a lot to be said about what went right in Aaron Boone’s decision-making and what eventually backfired to catalyze disaster.
There are many occasions when Boone stepped in at the right time to pull a pitcher and allowed the players to control their own destiny from the plate. He is most confident when he’s defending his guys from the dugout and isn’t afraid to get in an umpire’s face after a bad call. This has always been Boone’s style, and he continued his fiery streak this season with five ejections during regular season games. However, as manager, he is mandated to take accountability for some of the questionable decisions that may have put the Yankees in tougher situations.
MLB insiders Jon Heyman and Joel Sherman recently invited Joe Girardi to assess Boone’s decisions, and the former Yankees manager had a lot of positive takeaways despite a disappointing end to this season. Girardi even went on to claim that this was Boone’s best year of managing in his nine years on the job.
To give him credit, Boone had to navigate through several injuries this season and consistently found ways to keep the Yankees fighting for a playoff spot when all seemed lost, especially without Aaron Judge. Along with the Yankees captain, several star players had lengthy stints on the injured list, including Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Ryan Weathers, and Giancarlo Stanton. Expected 2026 contributors Cody Bellinger, Austin Wells, Trent Grisham, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. all missed a few weeks, too. Despite all the setbacks, Boone still found a way to propel the Yankees to their third conseuctive season of at least 93 wins, and he could’ve matched the 94 from both 2024 and 2025 had a rainout not nixed Game 162.
Contrast this to 2023, when Judge also missed a bunch of time and the Yankees struggled to 82 wins, their worst year in over two decades. Although the personnel may have just been better this time around, Boone did help keep the season from falling apart and rendering September irrelevant (let alone October). Credit Boone and pitching coach Matt Blake for helping the bullpen beat preseason expectations as well; others might not have had the confidence in unheralded names like Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, but they had strong seasons setting up for closer David Bednar.
The Yankees skipper also deserves some praise for refusing to put Judge in a spot where he could put his future career at risk. After being sidelined for the final stretch of the regular season with a moderate grade right calf strain, Judge was eager to get back into the lineup as the Yankees prepared for the postseason. Boone and general manager Brian Cashman ultimately decided to leave him off the roster for the Wild Card Series against Boston, which didn’t end up being an issue as the Yankees scored a combined 18 runs in the two-game dusting.
The Division Series was an entirely different scenario. On the advice of the Yankees’ medical staff, Judge was again absent from the series, in which the first two games were played on the turf at Tropicana Field. Judge, much like the rest of the Yankees’ offense, struggled to put up big numbers in Tampa Bay and went a combined 2-for-10 with a home run, four RBIs, and four strikeouts this season. He appeared disgruntled at Boone’s decision to keep him off the field for the series, but it may have been the best choice to allow him more time to recover from the calf injury and not put his career at risk — after all, severe Achilles injuries have been linked to the soleus muscle, which is where his calf was strained.
On the other hand, one of Boone’s most glaringly disappointing choices was putting Grisham in a leadoff spot in an elimination game when the Yankees were at risk of getting swept by the Rays on their own turf. Grisham, who barely saw any action in September, was the last of the batters left to keep the fight alive down 4-3 in the bottom of the ninth. With the hottest hitter of the postseason on deck in Ben Rice—who had been batting leadoff—Grisham ended up striking out in four pitches from Bryan Baker, allowing Tampa Bay to celebrate advancing to the ALCS from the Bronx clubhouse once again. With Grisham putting the cherry on top of an embarrassing postseason performance, the Yankees also continued their postseason losing streak and remain winless on the road since the 2024 ALCS against the Guardians.
It looks like Boone is here to stay for at least another year, as his contract runs through the end of 2027. Hopefully the Yankees can make enough clever moves during this expectedly elongated offseason to put them in a better spot for next season.

A wise man once said you can’t predict baseball. That doesn’t stop us from trying. Ahead of every season, just about every baseball-related publication tries to glimpse the future and predict the outcome of the year ahead. And at the end of the year, we realize again and again how futile the exercise can truly be. Even for a season that develops according to expectations, there will always be contours to the road that you didn’t have mapped out.
The 2026 Yankees washed out to an AL East rival in the Division Series for the second straight year; not an unforeseen fate for a team that was largely running it back with a nearly identical roster. As such, as we mark off the biggest surprises of the season, that end result isn’t all you’ll find similar with the last time we did this exercise.
So, let’s get started. Who could’ve predicted…
…that Cam Schlittler would be this good, this quickly?
We all saw glimpses of the ace starter Cam Schlittler could be when he carved up the Red Sox in the winner-take-all Game 3 of last season’s Wild Card Series, but I don’t imagine anyone anticipated the 25-year old would become the top pitcher in the American League the following year. Cam’s 14 start-run in 2025 showed a pitcher with tantalizing talent but plenty of room for refinement—namely a 10.2 percent walk rate which is the calling card of volatile and inconsistent pitchers from sea to shining sea.
That makes it all the more incredible that Cam was not only incredibly dominant, but consistently so. Schlittler didn’t really have his first bad start until June, and lest you thought that would be the moment the other shoe dropped, he didn’t let his ERA climb above 2.26 from midsummer onward. The 1.95 mark he finished with was good for a bronze medal in all-time Yankee lore. And the command troubles he flashed as a rookie vanished—he struck out 239 batters and walked only 49, a nearly 5-to-1 ratio. As of this writing, Schlittler has not yet been given the Cy Young award, but it’s a foregone conclusion. Even my most bullish preseason prediction for him probably would not have ended with him accepting that hallowed honor, but he electrified everyone and surpassed every test in 2026.
…that the Yankees would not grab a catcher at the deadline?
The vibes around this team were going sour with the June rib injury to Aaron Judge—which kept him out until September, when a quad strain would sideline him for the all-too-short remainder of the season. Brian Cashman had to act to shore up a roster which was suddenly emitting about seven distress signals. He added more offense where he could, bringing aboard Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos while calling up reinforcements from the minors—more on them later.
Not included on his shopping receipt, however, was a catcher, which was seen as the Yankees’ biggest need. That, of course, was because of the abysmal year Austin Wells had been enduring to that point. Wells had managed just a .504 OPS through the first half—unplayably bad even if it accompanied his generally solid defense. But the task of adding a new backstop was quickly complicated by their own closest rivals, who added two of the best catchers on the market. The Red Sox made a splash by trading for Adley Rutschman from the Orioles, and the Rays dealt with the Marlins for Liam Hicks.
As the hours toward the deadline ticked down, the Yankees were stuck with a bunch of poor options. The Twins’ Ryan Jeffers was coming off a recent injury and would be expensive; so would Colorado’s Hunter Goodman. The other remaining names were lateral moves at best. So, the Yankee braintrust ultimately chose to stick with Wells.
Thankfully, this was a problem that ultimately sorted itself out, as Wells found his swing at long last in the second half. He actually became one of the more consistent bats for the Yankees in the final two months and played to a second-half .787 OPS, more than doubling his home run and RBI total in the process. Unfortunately, Wells’ season would conclude with one more surprise, and a deeply unpleasant one: getting thrown out at third trying to leg out a triple in ALDS Game 1.
…that calling up the rookies actually worked?
If you told me that Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr. would be key planks in the Yankees’ second half lineup, I would have assumed their season had completely gone down the tubes. Jones, the powerful but whiff-prone outfielder, had not made waves in his first little Major League stint, hitting .167 in May before being sent back down to Triple-A. Lombard, the precocious shortstop, was a known commodity in the field, but a mystery at the plate—and awfully young to be thrown into the most pressure-packed spot in the league: the little patch of dirt between second and third in the Bronx.
The aforementioned injury to Judge—and later an injury to Trent Grisham—quickly brought Jones back into the fold, and the lefty picked up three hits in his first game back in the Show. Jones raised his level in June, hitting to an .808 OPS before a second brief demotion; then Cody Bellinger got hurt and he came back again, this time for good. He didn’t set the world on fire at any point in his rookie year, but Jones proved he could be a productive Major Leaguer, for at least the few months they needed him to be one. Another surprise with Jones was the somewhat ridiculous reverse splits he put up: a 1.107 OPS against lefties as opposed to just .647 off righties.
Lombard received the call to the Majors directly after the Trade Deadline, as the Yankees searched for more talent to ignite their slumbering offense. In a memorable MLB debut, Lombard made a handful of stellar plays at short, then homered in his second Major League at-bat—the same night his brother Jacob went yard in the low minors. Lombard turned a great first game into a great first week, showing composure beyond his years and an advanced approach at the plate.
The 21-year old’s offensive numbers soon dipped to pedestrian levels, and he had his defensive hiccups as well. But he never relinquished the starting shortstop position, even when Anthony Volpe—whom the Yankees had surprisingly optioned to make room from Lombard—returned to the roster. He acquitted himself well in the playoffs as well, going 6-for-18 overall. While neither he nor Jones are looking like perennial All-Stars, they may yet become mainstays on a roster in need of retooling this offseason.
