item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Yankees won 93 games in a year in which superstar Aaron Judge played just 66 games. That’s not a bad total, but it feels like it could, and should, have been more. General manager and Senior VP Brian Cashman routinely builds contending teams, and he should get credit for that, but he and his staff should be aiming higher and doing more to bring the title back to the Bronx.
A Wild Card Series win against the Boston Red Sox was a nice way to start the postseason, but the sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays exposed many harsh realities that are directly tied to Cashman and his decisions.
For the Yankees, 93 wins is not enough. They need to be the best team in the division, because that would bring them additional benefits in postseason play, such as home-field advantage and a ticket straight to the AL Division Series. Everybody in the organization is responsible for how the season plays out, but the spotlight will always point to the head of baseball operations.
Offseason moves and decisions
Cashman didn’t have a particularly bad offseason, but there were some notable holes when the season started. He didn’t find proper replacements for the rehabbing Anthony Volpe and the underwhelming Ryan McMahon: the former ended up being demoted in early August when the organization promoted George Lombard Jr., and the latter posted a 78 wRC+ and just 0.5 fWAR in 124 games. Volpe eventually returned and played an important role in the stretch run and during the postseason.
Extending Trent Grisham a qualifying offer was seen as a moderate risk when it happened, but it was a reasonable one since the outfielder had hit a career-high 34 homers in 2025. The outfielder declined this year, particularly on defense, but at least it wasn’t a long-term commitment.
The trade for Ryan Weathers was universally acclaimed, and it was a good piece of business on Cashman’s part. He ended up posting career-bests in ERA (3.60), fWAR (2.5), and innings pitched (137.1). The executive also brought back Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, Amed Rosario, Paul Goldschmidt, and Cody Bellinger.
Some of them were nice additions, particularly the 2019 NL MVP, but Cashman left the roster exposed to injuries and underperformance in many spots, and that’s on him, too. The bullpen was a bit thin, as some of his past trade experiments, such as Jake Bird, Ángel Chivilli, and Camilo Doval, just didn’t work. The same can be said about Rule 5 pick Cade Winquest. We are more than willing to give Cashman a pass in the bullpen, since the unit finished with the second-best ERA in MLB, though.
Trade Deadline activity (or lack thereof)
The Bombers entered the deadline with a few notable needs, which Cashman was very much aware of. They could have used a catcher given Austin Wells’ season-long slump up to that date, a reliever or two, a starter, and a right-handed outfielder.
They flirted with several backstops, but ended up empty-handed on that front to the frustration of fans. They did bring in Luis García Jr., who had been enjoying an amazing year in Washington with 23 homers and a 133 wRC+.
Heliot Ramos’ arrival was met with mixed reviews, and he posted a disappointing 93 wRC+ in pinstripes. He did have a 184 wRC+ vs. lefties during his time in the Bronx, which was one of the main reasons behind his acquisition. Giving up left-handed pitching prospect Henry Lalane to get him hurt, though. Speaking of…
Prospects and young core
Yes, you could say that the Yankees’ deadline was a disappointment, although some might disagree. However, they managed to keep most of their top prospects, including Lombard, Dax Kilby, Carlos Lagrange, Elmer Rodríguez, and Ben Hess. The promising Lalane was the lone exception.
They represent, together with Cam Schlittler, Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, Weathers, and Will Warren, the next wave of young talent that will, theoretically at least, keep the team highly competitive for the next 3-7 years. Keeping them all, particularly Lombard when half the league was asking for him in trade conversations, was a win for Cashman.
The rest of the farm, however, needs work. A lot of work. The Yankees will need to draft well and be active in the international market in the next couple of years to revamp their depleted system. At least Cashman took a step towards solving the situation, dismissing longtime international scouting director Donny Rowland and replacing him with Mario Garza in January.
Player development wins and losses
As every general manager, Cashman had some player development wins and losses when looking at the final picture of the 2026 campaign. He and his staff managed to turn Blackburn into a very useful reliever with his 1.59 ERA in 85 innings, and he got a nice season from Weathers, too.
Schlittler took a step forward into stardom, and Brent Headrick and Warren also improved in 2026. On the other hand, they couldn’t fix Doval, Luis Gil, McMahon, or Volpe, and Jasson Domínguez remains a fringe player. Grisham and Wells were also subpar for their standard.
The offense, generally speaking, had a mediocre year with a 101 wRC+ that ranked 14th in MLB. Yes, injuries to Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and other key hitters certainly hurt, but the feeling is that Cashman could have done better, or more.
We have said it multiple times in this space: the Yankees need new voices. They need to listen to more prepared people. They can’t keep doing the same things in personnel decisions, player analysis, research and development, and scouting and expect different results. Unless the ownership decides to part ways with their longtime executive, it will be on Cashman to push that change within the organization: does he have that in him, though? It’s at least a fair question.

item.content:encoded:
Let's call it like it is: Aaron Judge repeatedly insisting that he was in better shape than Aaron Boone was portraying all postseason long was weird. It got weirder when Brian Cashman went on record that using Judge in the ALDS "wasn't a choice," as he was too compromised to participate; Judge pushed back on that notion as well.
And yes, no matter what they say, it was also odd that he didn't appear in pregame intros before the Yankees' Wild Card battle with the Red Sox. "I think he was getting treatment stuff," Boone explained in the aftermath.
After the Yankees' elimination, Judge provided mostly platitudes amid the injury pushback. When pressed about his desire to go "all in" and whether the Yankees have fulfilled it, he did hesitate a bit, but then dropped a fairly non-controversial semi-banger.
“It’s tough to say,” Judge responded. “I want to trade for everybody, sign everybody every single year, but I know that’s not realistic. So they give us a winning team every single year, but that’s not good enough here in New York. We’re the Yankees. You’ve got to go out there and chase championships and go all in every year. So I’m excited to see what they do.”
The Yankees' brass didn't find it as "non-controversial" as we did, though. According to Jon Heyman, "Yankee bosses" weren't thrilled by Judge's characterization of the Yankees' spending around him. Those "bosses" believed that they'd done Judge's bidding by bringing Cody Bellinger home at the price he cost.
Aaron Judge's war of words with Yankees executives is now back in his court
It was Judge who said, "I hope we can run them back" regarding both Bellinger and Trent Grisham after the Yankees' elimination in 2025, and the Bellinger cold war seemed like it would be inevitably resolved in large part because of Judge's presence and preferences (he was also the right fit, and the Yankees' outfield would've been barren without him).
But Judge's comments this time around weren't heightened much above the generic "We're the Yankees, and we have to win" level. If team executives were frustrated by his insinuation that what we just saw wasn't good enough, then we have a problem here.
Then again, certain Yankees perceived as Judge favorites over the years either overstayed their welcomes or were given outsized roles past the point of expiration (Alex Verdugo).
Regardless, the ball is now in Judge's court as this bizarre battle of leaks continues into an offseason where the Yankees can ill afford in-fighting, especially with a lockout threatening to close off primary sources of communication.

Image Press Agency/Depositphotos
Jazz Chisholm Jr. discusses Judge's message
New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. discussed Aaron Judge's leadership after the Tampa Bay Rays completed a three-game American League Division Series sweep on October 7, 2026, at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx.
New York lost the deciding Game 3 by a 4-3 score. Chisholm said the captain addressed teammates following elimination, offering encouragement to a clubhouse whose postseason ended after five games against Boston and Tampa Bay.
Conor P. Fitzgerald/Shutterstock.com
Aaron Judge keeps teammates focused
Jazz Chisholm Jr. described Aaron Judge as a captain who speaks to teammates regularly, not only when the Yankees lose. He said those conversations helped players maintain a positive outlook during challenging moments throughout 2026.
Chisholm emphasized that Judge encouraged the group to stay focused on the right path. The second baseman's comments described an established clubhouse role rather than a new strategy introduced after Tampa Bay's October playoff series.
JHVEPhoto/Depositphotos
Aaron Judge misses the entire postseason
Aaron Judge missed all five New York Yankees postseason games in 2026, including both September Wild Card Series contests against Boston. The captain remained unavailable for October's Division Series because of a right calf strain.
Judge last appeared on September 16 and went on the injured list three days later. Manager Aaron Boone said the outfielder needed additional running drills and greater endurance before he could return to game action.
Conor P. Fitzgerald/Shutterstock.com
Aaron Judge records 18 homers in 2026
Aaron Judge appeared in just 66 regular-season games for New York in 2026, batting .241 with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs. A fractured rib and subsequent calf strain limited his time in the lineup.
Judge also posted a .360 on-base percentage and a .511 slugging percentage across his limited schedule. The rib injury kept him sidelined for more than three months before his eventual return in early September 2026.
Conor P. Fitzgerald/Shutterstock.com
Jazz Chisholm Jr. questions home boos
Jazz Chisholm Jr. heard boos from home fans at Yankee Stadium after fouling out as a seventh-inning pinch hitter in Wednesday's Game 3. The reaction came during New York's attempt to keep its postseason alive.
Chisholm said the reaction confused him because teammates were competing to win the deciding game. He added that the criticism did not hurt him and questioned why supporters would discourage players during a playoff contest.
andykazie/Depositphotos
Anthony Rizzo disputes Chisholm's remarks
Former Yankees first baseman Anthony Rizzo challenged Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s response to the home crowd's boos. On the Ross and Rizzo Unfiltered podcast, he questioned why a player familiar with New York would express surprise.
Rizzo noted that Aaron Judge, Anthony Volpe, and Giancarlo Stanton had also faced unfavorable reactions from home crowds. He viewed that history as evidence that players should better understand the city's particularly demanding baseball culture.
lev radin/Shutterstock.com
Aaron Boone makes a late lineup change
Yankees manager Aaron Boone benched Jazz Chisholm Jr. for Game 3 and started Anthony Volpe at second base. Chisholm said he discovered the change when he saw the lineup card rather than through a conversation.
Before the September Wild Card Series opener against Boston, Boone had sent Chisholm an encouraging text about his role. After Wednesday's Rays game, the infielder said direct advance notice of benching would have been preferable.
Dariozg/Depositphotos
Jazz Chisholm Jr. finishes with 41 steals
Jazz Chisholm Jr. finished the 2026 regular season with a .231 batting average, 19 home runs, 55 RBIs, and 41 stolen bases in 137 games. His final totals fell short of his previously stated ambitions.
Chisholm had targeted 50 home runs and 50 steals. Against Tampa Bay in the Division Series, he went hitless in eight at-bats, drew one walk, and recorded two stolen bases across all three postseason games.
sfStudio/Depositphotos
Drew Rasmussen limits Yankees to one hit
Tampa Bay starter Drew Rasmussen held the Yankees to one hit across eight scoreless innings on October 3. He recorded 10 strikeouts and earned a 1-0 victory in the Division Series opener at Tropicana Field.
New York catcher Austin Wells broke up Rasmussen's no-hit attempt with a double in the eighth inning but was retired trying for third base. That lone hit established a franchise postseason low for Yankees batters.
AlexanderMils/Depositphotos
Yankees commit four errors in Game 2
The visiting Yankees committed four fielding errors in their 5-2 Game 2 loss to Tampa Bay on October 5. Three defensive mistakes came in the first inning, when the Rays scored once at Tropicana Field.
Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s throw went wide of first base during a fielder's choice, allowing Yandy Díaz to score. Ben Rice delivered both New York runs with two solo home runs, but Tampa Bay ultimately prevailed.
Fun fact: Before becoming Yankees teammates, Aaron Judge and Jazz Chisholm Jr. shared an unusual distinction: both appeared on MLB The Show video game covers, five years apart.
Keeton Gale/Shutterstock.com
Victor Mesa Jr. delivers decisive home run
Victor Mesa Jr. gave Tampa Bay a 4-2 lead with a two-run home run in the sixth inning of Game 3. The rookie connected against Yankees left-hander Max Fried at Yankee Stadium on October 7.
Fried allowed four runs and seven hits through 5 2/3 innings while recording seven strikeouts. Tampa Bay closer Bryan Baker secured the final out when he struck out Trent Grisham with Chisholm stranded on second.
ags1973/Depositphotos
Anthony Volpe loses homer after review
Anthony Volpe appeared to tie Game 3 with a two-run home run in the sixth inning, but officials overturned the call following a replay review. A spectator reached over the wall from the left-field seats.
Officials determined the ball would neither clear the fence nor be caught without interference. Volpe received an RBI double, allowing George Lombard Jr. to score and narrowing Tampa Bay's advantage to 4-3 in Game 3.

Aaron Judge urges Yankees to improve roster
Aaron Judge urged Yankees leadership to strengthen the roster following the team's postseason exit. The captain called on managing general partner Hal Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman to consider changes before the 2027 season.
Chisholm said he wanted to remain with New York as free agency approached. The Yankees recorded 93 regular-season victories in 2026 but have not won a World Series title since 2009.

Another MLB season has ended in disappointment for the New York Yankees. Despite entering the postseason with championship aspirations, the Yankees fell well short of expectations, suffering an early exit against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS. Now heading into the offseason, the front office is preparing for what could be a summer of major roster turnover.
A report from The New York Post‘s Joel Sherman indicates that third baseman Ryan McMahon could be among those on the move. “The Yankees will try hard to find a way to redirect McMahon’s money elsewhere as they look to improve the roster for 2027,” Sherman reported.
Sherman noted that moving McMahon is primarily a financial decision rather than a reflection of his play, as the veteran remains a valuable asset at third base. Still, after another underwhelming campaign, the Bronx Bombers must weigh every available option to clear payroll flexibility and reshape their roster.
Meanwhile, additional reports suggest the Yankees could turn their attention toward outfield help, potentially targeting Seattle Mariners star Randy Arozarena. Offloading McMahon’s contract would give New York the financial room needed to pursue Arozarena and other high-profile targets as they aim to bounce back in 2027.
Ryan McMahon #19 of the New York Yankees fields a bunt.
Losing McMahon could leave the Yankees with a major infield void
Ever since acquiring McMahon from the Colorado Rockies, the Yankees relied on him to anchor third base. Moving on from the veteran leaves a massive defensive hole at the hot corner, with no clear internal prospects ready to take over.
McMahon’s offense cratered after leaving Denver for the Bronx, as he slumped to a .216 batting average with negligible WAR production across the 2026 season. Trading or releasing him would represent a clear cut-your-losses move, allowing New York to wipe his remaining $16 million salary for 2027 off the books.
If the Yankees part ways with McMahon alongside free-agent decisions surrounding Jazz Chisholm Jr., general manager Brian Cashman faces an immediate offseason burden: securing external trade targets or free agents to fill multiple spots in the starting lineup.
Key takeaways
- Ryan McMahon may be moved by the Yankees to clear payroll for 2027.
- Clearing McMahon’s salary would help New York pursue Seattle outfielder Randy Arozarena.
- Offloading McMahon leaves a $16 million salary gap and an unfilled third-base position.

How active will the New York Yankees be in trade this offseason??
After a disappointing 2026 campaign, it’s fair to assume the Yanks’ front office will be doing everything to better set up the roster for the 2027 season, which means meaningful trades could be on the horizon.
One recent trade rumor suggests the Yankees could be a player in a deal for Houston Astros shortstop Jeremy Peña.
More MLB on Heavy: Yankees Urged to Trade for Rangers’ All-Star Infielder
Would the Yankees Trade for Jeremy Peña?
Recently, FanSided.com’s John Perotto put out a trade rumors/free agency predictions piece for some of MLB’s biggest stars, and the MLB writer predicts the Yankees will trade for Jeremy Peña:
“Prediction: Traded to Yankees for outfielder Heliot Ramos, right-hander Brendan Beck and shortstop Dax Kilby (Yankees’ No. 2 prospect, MLB’s No. 36)”
He also wrote (about why Peña could be a hot commodity this offseason);
“Peña etched his name in Astros history in 2022, when he was the MVP of both the ALCS and World Series as a rookie. However, Peña’ time in Houston could be well over, as he is eligible for free agency at the end of next season and will likely earn at least $13 million through arbitration. Plenty of teams will be interested in a 29-year-old shortstop who hit .277/.325/.477 with 22 home runs and 12 stolen bases in 112 games,”
It creates an interesting question that the Yankees would have to solve with George Lombard Jr. and Jeremy Peña on the same side of the diamond.
Peña has a strong arm, so if the Yankees didn’t want to mess with the development of George Lombard Jr., they could move Peña to third, and leave Lombard Jr. at short, but this is a trade scenario where the Yankees could kill a couple of birds with one stone by offloading Heliot Ramos (who was disappointing since being traded to New York), and finding a much-needed 3B with strong production with the bat.
One rebuttal to the trade idea that’s worth mentioning is that this is quite a large trade haul for the Yankees to give up for a potential rental addition, so in order to justify the trade, New York would have to ink Peña to a contract extension at some point after *potentially* trading for him.

Taking a Closer Look at Jeremy Peña….
Jeremy Peña has quietly been one of the game’s most productive infielders over the past several seasons.
He’s a tenured 5-year MLB veteran with 680 games played.
Across those 680 games, and 2640 total at-bats, Pena is batting .272 with 86 home runs, 303 RBI, and 76 stolen bases.
His lifetime OPS+ is 109, but he’s coming off a strong 2026 campaign, where his OPS+ was 126.
In the past two seasons, Peña has logged an OPS+ north of 125.
Yankees fans, would you consider making this trade?? Why or why not??
And if not, who would you like to see Brian Cashman and company try to acquire this offseason?

Decisions, decisions.
For the New York Yankees this offseason, the front office has several decisions to make regarding retaining players who are set to hit the open market in free agency.
One of those big decisions for Brian Cashman and company is with 7X MLB All-Star infielder Paul Goldschmidt, who has indicated he would like to play in the 2027 season, but will it be with the New York Yankees?
More MLB on Heavy: Anthony Volpe Sounds Off On New York Yankees with 2-Word Message
Yankees Predicted to Let Paul Goldschmidt Walk in Free Agency
Paul Goldschmidt is coming off a solid campaign with the Yankees in 2026.
The 7x All-Star batted .252 with 18 home runs, 87 hits, 52 RBI, and an OPS+ of 111.
However, FanSided.com's Adam Weinrib recently urged that the Yankees should part ways with Goldschmidt:
"The Yankees have collected DH/first basemen like talismans all season, rotating Ben Rice and Luis Garcia Jr. and likely needing room for some Aaron Judge first base reps next year. Goldy has been a consummate professional. Every time you thought he was done contributing, he found an additional layer. But he's 39 years old. The Yankees value flexibility and probably don't want to roster a lefties-only first base backup."
Aside from Goldschmidt, the Yankees will also have decisions to make with players such as Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trent Grisham, and David Bednar/Paul Blackburn.
It could be an entirely new-looking Yankees squad in 2027, but speaking to Goldschmidt's free agency status, it feels like a toss-up if he will be back with the team or not. Ben Rice has emerged as the everyday first baseman for New York, and if that means Goldschmidt would get significantly less at-bats, why should Cashman commit to him for a one-year pact?
Perhaps the 39-year-old infielder would rather sign with a team like the St. Louis Cardinals in a reunion deal, which would allow him to see some time as a platoon DH.

Paul Goldschmidt is Likely Headed for Hall of Fame
While his production has slowed a little bit over recent seasons, Goldschmidt is likely headed for the Hall of Fame.
Across 16 years and 2179 games played, the 39 y/o has 390 home runs, 490 doubles, 1284 RBI, and a lifetime batting average of .286.
He was once considered the best first baseman in all of MLB, which led to the Yankees bringing him in before the 2025 season, and he's found some resurgence in his career since joining New York.
It will be very interesting to see the approach that the Yankees take during his free agency negotiations, and if the front office considers bringing him back.

Luis Garcia Jr. proved in 2026 that he's an intriguing piece for the New York Yankees' future, at least in the short term. The 26-year-old hits free agency following the 2027 season, so the Yankees will get one more look to see if they want to sign him long-term.
The issue with Garcia isn't his talent, but rather his fit on the roster. In his desperate quest to augment the offense at the trade deadline, Brian Cashman created a logjam of sorts. In the field, Garcia Jr. shares the same position as break out star Ben Rice. While one of them can DH, it's not an ideal solution.
New York has Giancarlo Stanton under contract for 2027, and should also give strong consideration to at least semi-regular DH days for Aaron Judge moving forward. There are only so many at-bats to go around.
Aaron Boone has a solution. Just change Garcia Jr.'s position.
“Obviously, an infielder in his [Garcia Jr.'s] past, and feel like that could even be in play, you know, moving forward in coming years,” Boone said via Brendan Kuty of The Athletic.
What Boone is referring to is Garcia Jr.'s history as a shortstop-turned-second baseman. Garcia Jr. never really stuck at short, playing just 70 career games at the position, with the majority coming in 2022. Since then, he has been a second baseman almost exclusively until this year.
With Jazz Chisholm Jr. hitting free agency and seemingly destined to leave, it seems like a perfect fit to just slide Garcia Jr. over and cross that need off the offseason list. The problem is that Garcia Jr. moved to first because he was miserable defensively at the keystone.
Trying Luis Garcia Jr. out at another position isn't out of the question, but the Yankees need a backup plan
Solving the offensive logjam and finding a way to get Garcia Jr., Rice, Judge, and possibly Stanton into the lineup at the same time is important, but it all falls apart if Garcia Jr. gives back everything he produces in the field. We've seen how badly New York's shoddy defense can derail their plans, with Game 2 of the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays serving as exhibits A through Z.
Simply put, the Yankees' defense needs to get better, not worse. But notice how Boone didn't name a position for Garcia Jr.? He just mentioned that they might be able to try some different things out due to the former Washington National's perceived versatility.
That's led to some fans on social media clamoring for New York to give him a shot at third base. While not exactly the same, range hasn't been an issue for Garcia Jr. at first, with him posting three outs above average and two defensive runs saved at the cold corner this year. The question will be whether or not his arm can hold up there.
The Yankees are unlikely to spend big at third base. Ryan McMahon has been a complete black hole at third base, as few hitters in the league can match his ineptitude at getting on base and avoiding strikeouts. Defense was once his calling card, but that fell off in 2026, too, with him recording -3 DRS and 0 OAA. He's owed $16 million in 2027, the final year of his contract. We can only hope that the Yankees decide to cut bait and just eat that money over the winter.
The problem is Garcia Jr. likely needs a platoon partner, and given that this kind of position change would be a roll of the dice, they'd need to find someone who not only hits right-handed, but could move into the position full-time and not be completely over his head should the experiment fail. Unfortunately, the third base free-agent market is pretty bare.
At the end of the day, this is an intriguing option for the Yankees, but not one that they can bank on. Putting all of their chips on Garcia Jr. playing a position that he has either proven he already isn't good at or has never played before, without a reasonable backup plan, is inviting an unnecessarily combustible situation.

The biggest question the New York Yankees are facing this offseason is what will happen with their manager, Aaron Boone.
In the immediate aftermath of the Yankees being eliminated from the MLB playoffs, there haven't been any official reports about Boone's status with the organization, but the rumor mill is certainly swirling, and there's plenty of speculation regarding candidates who could replace Aaron Boone.
One potential option is Don Mattingly, who is extremely familiar with the Yankees organization, being that he played in Pinstripes for 10+ seasons.
However, in a recent think piece by FanSided.com's Pat Ragazzo, the MLB writer notes that adding Mattingly to the staff may not be the move that solves all issues for the Yankees.
More MLB on Heavy: Anthony Volpe Sounds Off On New York Yankees with 2-Word Message
MLB Writer Urges Yankees to be Cautious with Don Mattingly as Boone Replacement
Again, there hasn't been any indication that Aaron Boone won't be the Yankees skipper in 2027, but fans have steadily been calling for him to be fired due to the fact that this recent ALDS loss felt very synonymous with how the Yankees have been eliminated in recent seasons (aside from the 2024 World Series run).
"Despite having a successful playing career with the Yankees, Mattingly isn't as well equipped as Boone to be managing in New York. Boone has extensive managerial experience in New York, and Mattingly only lasted five seasons with the Dodgers in Los Angeles. If Mattingly came back to the Bronx as the skipper and faltered, it could hurt his legacy with the Yankees."
Ragazzo also notes that since Aaron Boone has one year left on his contract, he's likely to stay with the Yankees for at least one more season.
And as for Mattingly, he's still in the running to become the full-time manager for the Phillies, although Philadelphia is expected to have an open managerial search.
Mattingly spent his entire 14-year career with the Yankees and was a six-time MLB All-Star and former AL MVP.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Make Interesting Roster Move Following MLB Playoff Elimination
What's Next for New York Yankees if Aaron Boone Remains the Skipper?
It's hard to fault Aaron Boone for the lack of offense the Yankees displayed against the Rays, but I think most of the New York fans are displeased with the same hamster-wheel cycle that has been the Aaron Boone experiment since he was hired.
However, if he is to remain the Yankees skipper, Brian Cashman is likely to make a handful of moves that will make this Yankees roster look a whole lot different once 2027 rolls around.
Cashman has decisions to make with players such as Paul Goldschmidt, Trent Grisham, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and a few pitchers.
The good news for the Yankees is that their starting rotation will remain intact, and Aaron Judge should play (if all goes well) a lot more than he did in 2026.
The Yankees remain at the forefront of major storylines in MLB as the offseason nears, and Aaron Boone's status will be a well-documented topic until a final decision is made on his future with the organization.

item.content:encoded:
Si viviera, George Steinbrenner estaría despidiendo gente.
Los Yankees de Nueva York fracasaron por 17ª temporada consecutiva en su intento de ganar un título de la Serie Mundial y vieron a un rival celebrar en su parque en octubre por tercer año seguido.
Steinbrenner, su tempestuoso propietario controlador de 1973 a 2008, se enfurecía por fracasos mucho menos frecuentes.
“Hay un estándar para ganar un campeonato. Es blanco y negro. No hay zona gris", reconoció el capitán de los Yankees, Aaron Judge, el miércoles por la noche, después de que Tampa Bay completó una barrida de tres juegos en la serie divisional de la Liga Americana sobre Nueva York. "Esto se relaciona con todos los días que te presentas a trabajar; cada cosita que haces es: ¿estás trabajando hacia un campeonato o no?”.
Nueva York ocupaba el cuarto lugar de las Grandes Ligas en carreras, el 13º en promedio de bateo y el segundo en OPS hasta el 31 de mayo, su último juego antes de que Judge ingresara a la lista de lesionados por una fractura de costilla. Del 1 de junio hasta el final de la temporada, los Yankees fueron 24tos en carreras, 29nos en promedio de bateo y 27mos en OPS. Judge regresó para siete juegos del 8 al 16 de septiembre, bateando para .174 con tres carreras impulsadas antes de que una distensión en la pantorrilla terminara su campaña.
Después de batear para .382 con 18 carreras en una barrida de dos juegos sobre Boston en la serie de comodines, los Yankees tuvieron un promedio de .130 y fueron superados 10-5 por Tampa Bay, con una alineación sin colmillo y sin el tres veces Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana.
“Miren, se trata de Aaron Judge, el mejor pelotero del mundo", indicó el mánager Aaron Boone. "Y es una ausencia enorme, enorme”.
Diez jugadores podrían quedar libres
El cerrador de los Yankees David Bednar, el segunda base Jazz Chisholm Jr., el jardinero central Trent Grisham y el primera base Paul Goldschmidt podrían convertirse en agentes libres antes de la próxima temporada, junto con el infielder dominicano Amed Rosario, los zurdos Tim Hill y Ryan Yarbrough, y los derechos Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber y Michael Fulmer.
“Aquí es donde quiero estar. Me encanta ser un Yankee. Crecí como fanático de los Yankees; desde las Bahamas, veía a Derek Jeter y a esos tipos todos los días", relató Chisholm. "Fue un gran momento ser un Yankee. Me encantó mi tiempo con los Yankees”.
Chisholm se enteró de que iría a la banca para el tercer juego contra los Rays, reemplazado por Anthony Volpe, cuando vio la tarjeta de la alineación.
“Siempre prefiero una conversación”, comentó.
El liderazgo parece estable
Brian Cashman completó su 29ª temporada como gerente general, al finalizar un contrato de cuatro años. En febrero de 1998, cuando asumió el cargo, marcó el 15º cambio de gerente general desde que Steinbrenner compró los Yankees en enero de 1973.
Boone terminó su novena temporada como mánager y le queda una campaña de una extensión de contrato por dos años acordada en febrero de 2025. Ha llevado a Nueva York a un récord de 790-565 en temporada regular y a tres primeros lugares en el Este de la Liga Americana, pero con una marca de 27-30 en playoffs.
“Sí, por supuesto”, respondió cuando le preguntaron si quería regresar para 2027. “Eso es para otro día”.
Judge pediría que se invierta dinero
Nueva York abrió la temporada con la tercera nómina más alta de las Grandes Ligas, 303 millones de dólares, y los Yankees atrajeron a poco menos de 3,3 millones de aficionados en 80 compromisos, cuarto en las mayores detrás de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, San Diego y Toronto.
Judge espera que Hal Steinbrenner, sucesor de su padre, indique a Cashman que sea activo en la búsqueda de un plantel de primer nivel.
“Somos los Yankees. Siento que deberían ir con todo y hacer lo que tengan que hacer y encontrar —si tenemos huecos, si se trata de encontrar a ciertos jugadores o personal, lo que necesitemos, hay que salir y conseguirlo", consideró Judge. "Por eso volví a firmar aquí para jugar con los Yankees: para pelear por un campeonato todos los años y apostar todo. Eso es lo que hago antes de cada campaña: prepararme para darle a este equipo y a esta ciudad todo lo que tengo, así que espero que ellos hagan lo mismo”.
Schlittler, un punto positivo
El derecho de 25 años Cam Schlittler probablemente ganará el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana después de terminar 14-6 con la mejor efectividad del Joven Circuito, 1,95, y 239 ponches en 193 2/3 entradas.
“No cumplimos con las expectativas de los aficionados y de esta organización”, reconoció. "Hay un cierto estándar de lo que significa ser un Yankee y no lo cumplimos”.

item.content:encoded:
A Yankees team entering the playoffs with the highest of expectations saw their season end with a 4-3 loss to an American League East rival in the ALDS at Yankee Stadium.
Their manager, Aaron Boone, emotions still raw from making the rounds in a disconsolate clubhouse, met with the media shortly after midnight to sort through it all.
“We'll continue to work at getting to that point where we're as complete in every department as we can be, offensively, pitching, defense,” Boone said. “They just outplayed us a little bit.”
Later, Boone would say: “In the end, you don’t move on usually when you can’t get enough big hits in a series.”
One can be forgiven if thinking this came out of Boone’s mouth after the Yankees fell to Tampa Bay Wednesday night in Game 3 of the ALDS, the franchise again failing to win its first World Series since 2009.
The above comments did indeed come out of Boone’s mouth…in early October of 2018 after a loss to the Red Sox in Game 4 of that year’s ALDS.
The remarks read familiar because here is some of what Boone did say, nearly eight years later to the date, after Wednesday night’s 4-3 loss to the Rays:
“We gotta be more complete offensively, defensively, pitching…they were a little bit better than us… ultimately didn’t swing the bats enough and put enough runs on the board to move on or to extend the series.”
If there has been a hallmark of Boone’s nine-year tenure, it has been taking clubs into the postseason seemingly with the pieces capable of an extended October run, only to come up short.
Often, as was the case this season – as well as in 2018, 2020, 2021 and 2025 – woefully so as those clubs failed to make even the ALCS (the 2023 Yankees missed the postseason entirely, Boone’s one playoff-less year).
This is not to focus solely on Boone, to whom the fan base has never truly warmed and whose unpopularity with it has steadily increased by the year.
Spoiler alert: there are no indications that owner Hal Steinbrenner has soured on Boone, who has one year remaining on his contract, or on Brian Cashman, the GM since 1998 whose contract expires at the end of this month, for that matter.
“Yeah, of course,” Boone said after Wednesday’s loss, asked if he expected to be back.
Though that could be read as an expression of the arrogance and condescension that occasionally creep into Boone press conferences, it should be read more as a reflection of working for owner Hal Steinbrenner. The Yankees' owner is generally loath to get rid of people with time and money left on their contracts, whether it be players, coaches or executives.
And, again, that isn’t to say if Boone’s contract was up at season’s end, Steinbrenner, consistently among Boone’s staunchest supporters over the years, would have any interest in pulling the trigger on a new manager search.
It is not anticipated Cashman will be going anywhere, either (though, separately, one does wonder if the 59-year-old executive, with the organization since his intern days of 1986 and in his current position for nearly 30 years, might at some point tire of the constant slings and arrows that come with the job and call it a day on his own).
No, the kind of changes in team hierarchy fans are clamoring for, and were clamoring for well before this most recent October flameout, remain highly unlikely.
Steinbrenner oversees an immensely successful baseball enterprise – success defined as annual playoff appearances, consistently high ratings on the YES Network and fans, from the late March/early April home opener through the end of September, streaming, proverbial wallets wide open for business, through the gates at Yankee Stadium to cheer on what is always one of the highest-paid teams in the game.
Winning the World Series is the goal, of course, and Steinbrenner, unfairly criticized for not being his bombastic father, George, very much wants to add trophy No. 28 to the franchise shelf. But, like the vast majority of his brethren now in MLB ownership, Steinbrenner is most concerned with “process.”
As long as “the process” – always treated with the utmost secrecy, lest it be subject to scrutiny of any kind – is deemed good and sound and profitable, the results, when measured in the win-loss column, become almost secondary.
That trickles from ownership on down and leads to Boone, back in 2018 and then again after Wednesday night’s game, saying things like the team vanquishing his was just “a little bit better.”
The Yankees, ever sure of their “process,” again were simply victimized by inconvenient injuries, a bad bounce, unable to get that elusive “big” hit, etc.
So, no need for true organizational self-introspection. No introspection that goes beyond throwing a member or two of Boone’s coaching staff to the wolves, or concluding an additional “war room” or two is needed behind the scenes for better implementation of said “process.”
Better that than acknowledging that the 2018 Red Sox were more than “a little bit better” than that year’s Yankees.
Just as the 2026 Rays were significantly better than the 2026 Yankees – both in the regular season and the postseason.
And on it goes.

Aaron Judge didn't play in the American League Division Series due to injury, but he spoke to the media following the New York Yankees' series-ending loss to the Tampa Bay Rays.
The Rays completed their ALDS sweep of the Yankees with a 4-3 win in the Bronx on Wednesday night. Victor Mesa Jr. hit the go-ahead home run for the Rays in the top of the sixth inning.
Even though Tampa Bay won the AL East, there were plenty of fans who expected a better fight from New York. Of course, it doesn't help that Judge missed the whole series due to a calf strain.
Following Wednesday night's season-ending loss, Judge was asked how general manager Brian Cashman and owner Hal Steinbrenner will react to the Yankees falling short of their ultimate goal yet again.
"We're the Yankees," Judge said. "I feel like they [the front office] should go all-in and do what they need to do. If we've got holes, if it's finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you've got to go out there and get it."
Clearly, Judge wants the Yankees to be more aggressive when it come to building the roster.
Expect changes for the Yankees.
For starters, the Yankees are expected to move on from a few veterans like Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham this offseason. The Bronx Bombers may have tipped their hand by having Chisholm on the bench for a do-or-die playoff game.
The Yankees also have to consider moving on from Ryan McMahon and Giancarlo Stanton in hopes of landing more reliable hitters.
Suffice to say, this will be a pivotal offseason in the Bronx.

Yankees' 'offseason focus' should include David Bednar, Paul Blackburn originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees have plenty of roster decisions to make before next season.
Whether to re-sign second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. for the foreseeable future may be the offseason's biggest question.
The Yankees don't need Chisholm, but there aren't many other options who offer more upside than him.
Concerning the pitching staff, general manager Brian Cashman has built a strong and very deep rotation. However, the bullpen may lose multiple key arms this winter.
Tim Hill, Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, John Schreiber, Michael Fulmer, and closer David Bednar will all become unrestricted free agents.
"Not only is this New York's biggest need, but it might also be just about their entire offseason focus," Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller wrote.
Plus, who knows what Fernando Cruz's status will be. The right-hander is attempting to recover from a partially torn UCL without surgery.
Keeping Bednar at closer should be Cashman's top priority in the bullpen.
"Bednar is the biggest one by far, owner of 35 saves and a 2.47 ERA this season. Like Chisholm, he could also be headed for a qualifying offer of an estimated $23.1M, but is expected to decline it in pursuit of something closer to a four-year, $66M contract," Miller added.
His value has skyrocketed, but the Yankees should also look to re-sign Blackburn. He went through dominant scoreless streaks and allowed just 16 earned runs in 85 innings.
Blackburn, who made a modest $2 million salary in 2026, struck out just 7.3 batters per nine innings.
Reshaping the bullpen will be a massive project for New York's front office, and retaining Bednar and Blackburn should be step one.

BRONX, NY — Forced to sit helplessly in the Yankees’ dugout and watch the Tampa Bay Rays execute a dominant ALDS sweep, another year of Aaron Judge in Pinstripes has come and gone without a championship.
Granted, this year was a little different. The 34-year-old slugger missed 96 games with a fractured rib and strained calf — the latter of which held him out for the entire postseason, regardless of his pleas to be included on both the Wild Card and ALDS rosters.
As this series against Tampa progressed, it became increasingly clear that even a 50% Judge would have been a better option than most of what manager Aaron Boone trotted out in each of the three games. The Yankees scored just five runs in three games, and the lineup construction fell under considerable fire, especially toward the end of Game 3 when Trent Grisham, who inexplicably was put in the lead-off spot, went down swinging to end the season with slugger Ben Rice standing on the on-deck circle with his bat on his shoulder.
Now, imagine if that was Rice leading off (and playing first base) and Judge in the DH spot?
“Look, it’s Aaron Judge, the greatest player in the world,” Boone said. “And that’s a huge person to be missing. But every team tends to deal with different attrition that they gotta face every year, and unfortunately that was for us much of this year.”
Judge had made it known in recent weeks that he was unhappy with some of Boone’s phrasing regarding his moderate calf strain, even the disclosure of the extent of his injury. Yet the two-time defending AL MVP is still riding with his manager, regardless of how hot people hope his seat might be.
“Yeah, he’s our manager,” Judge said. “He’s running this ship. He puts us in the right position to go out and succeed, especially a season like this where I’m banged up and missing 100 games, you miss [Giancarlo Stanton], [Gerrit] Cole, [Carlos] Rodon… For him to manage it the way he did and put us in the best position to get into the postseason and get an opportunity to win a World Series, he’s definitely had our back.”
The problem is that the Yankees’ roster simply was not good enough to be the best — or second, third, maybe even fourth team — in baseball. Owner Hal Steinbrenner’s frugality has constructed a roster with strong pitching, but poor defense and a lineup that offers virtually no support around a healthy Judge.
Rice is a great supporting piece, but there has to be far more than Cody Bellinger or Jazz Chisholm, or Austin Wells.
When asked whether or not Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman have gone all-in enough in hopes of breaking a now 17-year World Series drought, Judge came within a few feet of laying the blame on their shoulders, saying, “It’s tough to say.”
“I want to trade for everybody, sign everybody every single year,” Judge said. “But I know that’s not realistic. They give us a winning team every single year, but that’s not good enough here in New York. We’re the Yankees. You’ve got to go out there and expect championships and go all-in every year.”
The hope is that the philosophy finally changes this winter. There are not going to be any excuses after asset firm Apollo Financial provided a $2.6 billion cash infusion.
“We’re the Yankees. I feel like they should go all-in and do what they need to do,” Judge continued. “If we’ve got holes, if it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you’ve got to go out there and get it. That’s why I signed back here to play with the Yankees, to fight for a championship every single year and to go all-in. That’s what I do every offseason: get ready to give this team and this city everything I got. I expect them to do the same.”

item.content:encoded:
It would be perfectly understandable if that headline made you double check the box score to see if you somehow missed Heliot Ramos taking the field in the New York Yankees’ tough Game 2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. But it's the fact that the Yankees struggle to find any real use for Ramos that makes his trade a real disaster and a complete waste of a roster spot.
The Rays trotted out two lefty relievers in Game 2 in an attempt to neutralize the Yankees’ onslaught of left-handed bats. Cam Booser came in for Rays’ starting pitcher Freddy Peralta and he walked one heck of a tightrope to narrowly escape a fifth inning jam. After facing just two batters and recording only one out, Rays manager Kevin Cash decided to bring in LHP Ian Seymour to bridge the gap to closer Bryan Baker in the ninth.
Despite giving up a solo shot to Ben Rice in the eighth inning, Seymour tossed three spectacular innings and made sure he never gave the Yankees any hope of mounting a comeback. With the lineup filled with eight left-handed batters, the Yankees seemed to play right into Cash’s master plan.
You might assume that a player like Ramos would make for the perfect option to bring into the game in place of one of those lefty hitters. If you recall back at the trade deadline, Yankees GM Brian Cashman acquired Ramos for the exact purpose of becoming another one of the team’s weapons to combat left-handed pitching.
As Ryan Garcia of Just Baseball pointed out, the Yankees traded prospects Kaeden Kent and Henry Lalane to the San Francisco Giants to add Ramos to their roster. The Yankees thought highly enough of him to surrender Lalane, a top-five prospect in their system, in hopes he would provide some much-needed pop against lefties.
But with Paul Goldschmidt hitting for Ryan McMahon in the top of the eighth inning, he became the Yankees only pinch hitter of the game. Even as Luis García Jr. and Spencer Jones struck out in their at-bats against Seymour, Ramos never left the comfort of his own spot on the bench. If he couldn’t even be brought out for an at-bat against the Rays’ southpaws, why is he even on the ALDS roster for the Yankees?
Heliot Ramos never seemed like a good fit for the Yankees
With a .297/.383/.525 slash line against LHP in 2026, Ramos can rake. We can’t pretend that he isn’t a quality player for that skillset. He even had a brief redemption arc that made fans briefly think that the Yankees won the trade. But with a .651 OPS in 303 at-bats against right-handed pitchers this season, Ramos has gradually limited himself at the plate. His strength against LHP still makes him a very strong platoon player to have on a Major League roster. Just not the Yankees’ roster.
As a poor defender, Ramos is tough to justify penciling in the lineup as an outfielder. That means that he is best suited to fill in as a DH. But with Rice now almost exclusively serving as the Yankees’ full-time DH, Ramos will never steal at-bats away from the Yankees' best offensive player in 2026.
At the same time, Ramos’ lack of defensive prowess makes him a liability to have out there in the field with a team already famous for giving their opponent extra outs to play with. That leaves his only option as a pinch hitter against LHP. Even then, Yankees manager Aaron Boone couldn’t see the value in taking the bat out of the hands of anyone else in the lineup in Game 2.
That all but puts the final nail in the coffin for Ramos’ career with the Yankees. For a rebuilding team looking to add a solid hitter, he can provide solid value at the plate. For a playoff contending team looking for a platoon player to face off against LHP as their DH, Ramos can again provide solid value. But the Yankees have neither of those needs. And their Game 2 loss against the Rays’ lefties made that obvious.

The Wild Card Series came and went this year without much intrigue. The Yankees blew the Red Sox out of the water, the White Sox stuck the final stake into the dying heart of the Astros, and the Padres embarrassed the Cubs. None of those series were competitive, but there was one that at least reached a Game 3: the divisional battle between the Braves and Phillies.
For one side, it was a mental block that had to be erased. The Braves hadn’t won a playoff series since winning the World Series in 2021, and had lost to the Phillies in consecutive NLDS in 2022 and 2023 to springboard their latest contention window. It’s a win-now core, and even though they had a lot of issues, they weren’t a team that can accept a loss this early.
The other side couldn’t really accept that either: the Phillies had been eliminated earlier and earlier since a heartbreaking loss in the 2022 World Series. Their core was much older, with much less young talent to supplement it. They had stumbled into the playoffs with a disastrous final week that messed up their pitching. They had reached the point where most teams are at the end of their contention window. If you don’t show reason to believe in this core, it’s going to be dismantled.
The Braves won that grudge match in Game 3, sending the Phillies home with another disastrous season and ensuring no October baseball in the City of Brotherly Love for the first time in five years. It’s a sobering defeat for a team whose best players are past their prime, which has an interim manager, and which faces an extremely bleak outlook. Such a bleak outlook is solely because of one man and his ideas of roster construction: Dave Dombrowski.
At the same time that the Phillies and their brass were openly wondering what was next for the franchise, the Yankees were preparing to play Game 1 of the ALDS at Tropicana Field, which they lost last night in St. Petersburg. It came in the team’s 34th consecutive winning season and their ninth playoff appearance in the last 10 years.
Despite having a core of older veterans who do have a gradually closing window, like the Phillies, the Yankees found a lifeline in the development of two little-known prospects into the likely AL Cy Young and a slugging first baseman/DH who will get down-ballot MVP votes in his second full season. The much-maligned architect of this entire core, and several before it, is Brian Cashman.
Cashman and Dombrowski have spent a long time as adversaries. While he was no longer in charge, a roster full of players acquired under Dombrowski beat the dynasty Yankees in the 2003 World Series. His next team, the Tigers, beat the Yankees in the postseason in 2006, 2011, and 2012. His Red Sox took out the Yankees in 2018 en route to a World Series. You’d think the guy who has won all these head-to-head battles would be heads and shoulders above, but then you must wonder why he’s had to bounce around so much.
Here, what we really get is two entirely different executives with entirely different philosophies about how to build a contender. Neither has much experience overseeing failure, so the large part of their careers has been defined by their climb toward the top of the mountain.
With Cashman, as we’ve seen for essentially three decades, it’s an approach that is more focused on long-term sustainability. He’s been blessed with the power of working with one of the league’s deepest pockets in the biggest market in baseball, which usually allows him the bandwidth to fill crippling holes. His approach in the offseason is predicated on getting high-end talent on big deals in free agency to flex their financial muscle, but also making shrewd, under-the-radar trades to fill much of the roster.
While he’s willing to shell out for big contracts both via trade and in free agency and absorb the financial risk that he knows ownership can deal with, he’s more measured when it comes to truly taking that next step. You’ll see him balk at an additional year in a free-agent deal or hold onto a top prospect in trade discussions for a top-level talent. There are times this works, but there are also times he’s left at the altar and burned for it. Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s free agency and trade discussions for Gerrit Cole in the winter of 2017 ring a bell for that.
That restraint is based on his belief in long-term sustainability. The Yankees rarely have a great farm system, but if they can produce an era-defining superstar (hello, Aaron Judge), it makes everything drastically different for roster construction. By that note, he’ll always leave holes on the roster to allow for a cheap, homegrown player to fill them. From here, it can go two ways. You can get a Judge and some great complementary pieces on rookie contracts like Gleyber Torres and Gary Sánchez, but you can also get burned by hoarding a prospect in trade talks (Chance Adams, Clint Frazier, Deivi Garcia).
This mentality is completely different than the one you’ll see Dombrowski employ. His approach to roster building, while similarly predicated on a very generous owner with deep pockets, is more based on taking risks in both free agency and the trade market, pursuing as much proven talent as possible. This approach narrows a contention window, but it’s something he’s able to work off of. It’s a lot easier to do your job when you identify a five-year window to win and disregard anything that comes after it.
Looking at how he’s managed this throughout his tenure, he made some gigantic trades and signings to turn Detroit into a perennial AL contender, acquiring Miguel Cabrera from his old stomping grounds in Miami in 2007 and David Price in 2014, while also inking Prince Fielder to a ridiculous nine-year contract. In Boston, he made blockbuster signings in Price and J.D. Martinez while swinging a franchise-altering deal for White Sox ace Chris Sale. In Philly, he’s been more muted, but gave a massive 11-year deal to Trea Turner to solidify the shortstop position. You’re never bored in an offseason under Dombrowski.
This approach is predicated on doing whatever it takes to climb to the mountaintop, looking to increase the team’s chances of raising the Commissioner’s Trophy at least one time by enough that it offsets the losses that will come down the road. It’s risky in a sport that has so much randomness in the postseason, but if it pays off, it’s genius. Just ask the 2018 Red Sox, who proceeded to bottom out in the ensuing two seasons and only make one playoff appearance over the next six seasons, if they’d trade that title for more wins in those lost seasons.
When it doesn’t work? It leads to a lot of resentment. The Tigers won a pair of pennants in 2006 and 2012, but in an extended, decade-long run with the same core of Cabrera and Verlander at the forefront, the Tigers imploded, missing the playoffs in four consecutive years between those pennants and ultimately wound up spending over a billion and burning up the farm system for no World Series. After Dombrowski was dismissed after a terrible 2015 season, the Tigers wouldn’t make the playoffs again until 2024.
The Phillies hired him to be their President of Baseball Operations in 2020, and he did what he does best. He got Turner; he got Kyle Schwarber; he extended Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola. In lieu of blockbusters, he elected to slowly chip away at the farm depth by making a mountain of smaller moves every winter and summer. It was, honestly, his least all-in job as an executive since he was in Miami, but it’s still leading to the same place as Detroit. He was hailed as a savior in 2022 when the Phils won the pennant, but is now on the verge of being driven out of town as they stare down an unbelievably bleak future without a title to show for it.
The strengths and weaknesses of Cashman and Dombrowski are directly opposite of each other. They show the two ways you can run a perpetual contender. Cashman’s philosophy allows him to keep his job for decades and decades, while Dombrowski often gets canned after the contention window slams shut. You might think Cashman’s job security is a byproduct of organizational complacency, but there’s a reason he’s universally revered for his work in baseball circles.
The two rarely go head-to-head for big signings or trades, but you can imagine how they would go. Dombrowski might give a guy an extra year or two in a deal that Cashman is apprehensive about doing. It could either end up like Yamamoto, where his prime wins you multiple championships, or like Turner, who’s turning into one of the worst contracts in the sport just four years in. In the trade market, Cashman might balk at the asking price for a big-time player, while Dombrowski would go for it. That could lead to a massive success like Sale, or a massive failure like what the Mets did with PCA.
If Dombrowski ran the Yankees over the last 15 years, do we see a World Series? I’m not sure. I’d imagine he’d be much more interested in that mega-deal the Braves proposed in 2014 that would’ve sent Luis Severino, Sanchez, and Judge to Atlanta for a box full of proven talent. He’d also be much more likely to pull the trigger on a Kyle Tucker trade that included Ben Rice in the winter of 2024 or a Eugenio Suarez/Merrill Kelly deal with the D-Backs that would’ve sent Cam Schlittler to the desert.
All in all, as the Phillies enter an offseason where they must consider firmly shutting their contention window, the Yankees not only still have a chance to win this year, but seem to have enough young talent left over to win down the road when Judge and Gerrit Cole hang up their cleats. It’s the latest chapter evolving in the several decades that Dombrowski and Cashman have spent as two of the league’s most famous executives, a chess match to truly decide which is the better style of building a contender.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — This is an open letter to anyone who's railed against Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone over the years. That's a huge swath of Yankees fans – maybe all of them. So let's call this a mass mailing.
The Yankees are a step closer to the World Series for two reasons. The first was the Red Sox's glaring deficits. Scoring just two runs in 18 innings, they just weren't good enough to hang with the Yankees. If the Wild Card Series were replayed 10 times, the Yankees would likely win nine.
The second reason is why we're here today. Although this isn't the greatest Yankees roster of the last 20 years, it is remarkably well-constructed and well-managed. That's another way of saying Cashman and Boone have done their jobs well. They deserve credit for that.
The question is whether the critics will ever reconsider. I have my doubts. The folks who've been demanding Cashman's and Boone's firing for almost a decade aren't exactly open to reasonable dialogue. They're dug in so deep that one of them, who just happens to be an old college buddy, insisted, "Anyone could've beaten the Red Sox. That's how much they sucked."
My friend isn't entirely wrong — at least about Boston's non-existent offense. It's hard to believe this was the same team that went on a 14-game winning streak this summer.
But to suggest that any manager with Cam Schlittler as their ace and Ben Rice hitting lasers could've taken down the Sox is flat-out wrong. That's like saying all managers are the same. Their only job is to fill out the lineup card and talk to the TV cameras after the game.
Not quite.
Managers have personality traits that can enhance the roster's potential. Joe Torre, laid-back in a streetwise sort of way, was the perfect candidate to replace the hyper-involved Buck Showalter. Torre was never loud, but still tough enough to absorb late owner George Steinbrenner's manic behavior.
When Torre's enthusiasm for managing waned by 2006, Joe Girardi — ultra-prepared, obsessed with process — represented the pendulum swinging in the other direction. And when the next generation of Yankees decided Girardi was just too uptight and disconnected from the clubhouse, Boone won over Cashman because he was smart, calm and relatable.
I realize fans no longer care about Boone's personality. Not even his .582 winning percentage — second only to the Dodgers' Dave Roberts among active managers — gets the credit it deserves. What matters are championships. Boone has none since he replaced Girardi in 2018. In the Bronx, that's 0-for-forever.
That doesn't mean Boone is a bad manager. He checks so many other boxes that have kept the Yankees competitive. The players like Boone, but more importantly, they trust his instincts. In fact, Boone had a terrific series against Boston, embarrassing Chad Tracy, his counterpart in the other dugout.
Boone didn't make any significant mistakes against the Sox. His most important decision of the series came in Game 1.
After allowing Schlittler to throw 117 pitches, Boone summoned Paul Blackburn in the seventh inning to protect a 2-0 lead. Facing Ceddanne Rafaela with the tying run at the plate, Blackburn induced an inning-ending double play. The Yankees went on to score seven runs in the next two innings.
Tracy, on the other hand, made two decisions that doomed Boston. In both games, he pulled his starter in the fifth inning with two outs and the Sox trailing 1-0 — first Payton Tolle, then Sonny Gray. The Yankees promptly destroyed reliever Erik Miller on both occasions.
Several Sox players, including Gray and Willson Contreras, have since second-guessed Tracy's strategy and the team's overall direction.
You don't hear that kind of anti-Boone sniping in the Yankees' clubhouse. Even Boone's handling of Aaron Judge's irritation at being left off the Wild Card roster showed finesse. Boone demonstrated he was in control without making a show of pulling rank.
One former Yankee texted me the other day about the back-and-forth between Boone and Judge. He believes the episode showed how much Boone has grown on the job.
"All (Boone) said was, 'We don't expect Judge to be back,'" the former Yankee said. "That's Boone's way of telling the rest of the players, 'It's time for you to step up. Don't sit here waiting for Judge to rescue you.' It was a positive message."
Of course, it takes the right kind of players to understand that. The Yankees are a stable group. Even Jose Caballero, who came to the Yankees with the reputation of being a rogue element, has fallen into line.
That's where Cashman comes in. He made one right call after another in assembling this 93-win roster. The bullpen is airtight; the gamble on trading for closer David Bednar has worked to perfection. The GM made the smart move by promoting George Lombard Jr. this summer instead of waiting until September or 2027. And the rotation, finally healthy, is the Yankees' best since 2009.
MORE BY BOB KLAPISCH
All it took was one more piece — Max Fried. His signing in free agency in 2025 had Cashman's fingerprints all over it.
Beat the Rays, and the Yankees are back in the AL Championship Series. Win there, and they're back in the World Series for the second time in three years. At that point, those haters just might admit Cashman and Boone had something to do with it.
I'm such a nice guy that I'll give my friend a chance to admit he was wrong all along.

item.content:encoded:
Much was said about the New York Yankees and the way the front office, led by general manager Brian Cashman, went about its business at the trade deadline. Many believed the Bronx Bombers didn’t do enough to truly compete in the 2026 MLB Postseason, but that was proven wrong in the AL Wild Card against the Boston Red Sox—despite Aaron Judge’s absence. Amid the champagne celebration, starting pitcher Gerrit Cole voiced an honest assessment of the work done behind closed doors by the front office.
Although the true test will come when the Yankees play the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS next, the way the squad in The Bronx has been assembled clearly didn’t go unnoticed by Cole, who praised Cashman and the Yankees’ brass after the 2-0 series win over the Red Sox.
“You’ve got to go out and buy the tools. The roster looks really good at this point. We’re very competitive, and we have a lot of different ways that we can beat you. A lot of credit goes to a lot of people in this building,” Cole stated, via Chris Kirschner of The Athletic.
NY Yankees’ lineup depth proves decisive
It’s a new day in New York, more specifically in The Bronx. Indeed, the Yankees would love to have Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton back at the plate, but they have figured things out even without those two power bats.
Gerrit Cole #45 of the New York Yankees at Yankee Stadium.
New York is no longer a home-run-dependent creature in the MLB Playoffs. The Yankees are now a depth monster, ready to drown out opponents with lengthy, grueling innings, especially when playing at home at Yankee Stadium.
Yankees’ perfect 6th inning in Game 2
It remains to be seen how this strategy stacks up against the AL East-winning Rays, but it wreaked havoc against the Red Sox. The bottom of the sixth inning in Game 2 was Aaron Boone’s team’s magnum opus so far in the postseason. The Yankees made the most of every single thing the Red Sox gave them.
A wild pitch? Spencer Jones would run his way to first. Another bad throw, and he stole two bases, setting up shop at third. From there on, the Yankees’ batters simply kept the base hits coming until it was Cody Bellinger’s turn at the plate.
The Red Sox picked their poison: They intentionally walked Ben Rice to first base. Bellinger needed just one changeup from Garrett Whitlock to decipher the code. On the second pitch, he went yard, calling game in the process as New York jumped to a game-sealing, series-ending 8-1 lead.
NY Yankees are for real in 2026 postseason
It was the perfect demonstration of how the entire lineup can come together to decide postseason games for the Pinstripers. If they could, the Yankees would hang it up on a wall at Yankee Stadium, but they don’t do that in The Bronx.
All they care about is winning the World Series, and this Yankees team, with a different recipe from years past, confirmed it can be a serious contender for the Commissioner’s Trophy in 2026. And that’s even without Judge.
Lastly, Brian Cashman, who’s been through the wringer and at the receiving end of fans’ criticism time and again, deserves credit. It’s still early for victory laps, but Cole’s shoutout to the front office’s work was well deserved.
Key takeaways
- Brian Cashman received praise from Gerrit Cole after New York eliminated Boston.
- The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-0 in the AL Wild Card series.
- Cody Bellinger hit a game-sealing home run in the sixth inning of Game 2.

The Yankees have always insisted Spencer Jones was more than just a power hitter.
They also praised his quickness and athleticism.

It was that latter part that was on display in Wednesday’s Game 2 wild-card-clinching 9-2 win in The Bronx.
With the Yankees clinging to a two-run lead, Jones led off the bottom of the sixth against Garrett Crochet, one of the game’s premier lefty pitchers, just coming back from a five-month absence because of a shoulder injury.
Jones whiffed, but Crochet badly bounced the third strike, and it got away from Adley Rutschman.
Jones hustled down the line, and after initially being ruled out, reached first when the call was overturned.
“When he gets it going, he can really go,’’ Aaron Boone said.
The 6-foot-7 Jones then attempted to steal second, and Rutschman’s throw went into center, allowing Jones to get to third.
With the infield in, fellow rookie George Lombard Jr. drove in Jones with a single to spark a six-run inning.
“Speed is something I’ve always had,’’ Jones said. “I’m glad it worked out. It was a fun night.”
There have been a few of those lately for the 25-year-old, who has contributed in numerous ways down the stretch after getting off to a 4-for-24 start with 12 strikeouts in his first 10 games in the majors.
When Jones returned to The Bronx later in the season, he had improved his approach at the plate and showed he could hit in the majors.
Jim Hendry, special assistant to GM Brian Cashman — who was among the Yankee scouts who evaluated Jones while he was at Vanderbilt — said the fast development shouldn’t come as much of a surprise.
“Big guys like that, it takes them longer to adjust,’’ Hendry said prior to the game. “Sure, they’re gonna strike out a lot. They’ve got more holes to figure out how to fix. But you know when they do, they can be special.”
As Hendry noted, the Yankees “have always liked big players.”
Still, there aren’t many examples of players Jones’ size hitting well, with Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton being two exceptions.
Jones is trying to become another, and the Yankees have seen some promising signs in the second half of the season.
As they’ve dealt with the lengthy absence of Judge because of rib and calf injuries, multiple injuries to Trent Grisham, as well as another disappointing season from Jasson Domínguez, Jones has been thrust into an important role.
In Game 1, the Yankees went with the lefty-swinging Jones against left-hander Payton Tolle.
Shop Yankees Merch
He had a pair of solid at-bats against Tolle, and Aaron Boone said Wednesday that he considered having Giancarlo Stanton pinch hit for Jones to lead off the bottom of the seventh against another southpaw, Alec Gamboa.
Instead, Boone stayed with Jones, who singled.
Among the reasons Boone stuck with Jones was the success he’d had versus lefties in the majors — just part of what’s developing into a well-rounded game for the former first-round pick.
“It’s hard in the modern game to hit when you’re 6-foot-7,’’ Hendry said. “But when you do it well, you don’t have to worry about launch and other things. When you’re that big, the ball lifts itself. He’s still got a lot of work to do, but he’s becoming a good player already.”

Facing lefty Payton Tolle, this was a game reserved for a righty-hitting catcher. Maybe Ryan Jeffers, who might as well have been looking for a New York apartment considering the months of speculation. Or maybe the switch-hitting Adley Rutschman, another potential Yankees target who was behind the plate Tuesday because he was redirected instead to the Red Sox, who overwhelmed the Orioles with their trade package.
But Cashman did not pull the trigger on finding another catcher, even a complement, and so Wells — who had been among the worst hitters in baseball at that point — only saw his stranglehold on the starting job strengthen.
That move — or rather lack of move — sure looked smart when Wells took that second-inning at-bat and drove in the only run the Yankees would need.
The Yankees’ starting catcher (and with all due respect to Ali Sánchez, their only catcher) breathed even more life into his revitalized season in the Yankees’ 9-0 statement of a victory over Boston in The Bronx to move one win from an ALDS date with the Rays.
“By no means was it surprising,” Ben Rice said of Wells, who went from virtually unplayable to a catcher the Yankees will ride for as long as this postseason run lasts.
Before the Yankees ran away late in the game, their offense had started with promise but only promise: Prior to Wells stepping up for his first at-bat, the club had gone 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and was threatening to waste another opportunity. In the frame, George Lombard Jr. singled, moved to second on a one-out knock from Anthony Volpe and then watched as Spencer Jones fouled out for the second out.
But the lefty-hitting Wells — who batted .122 with a .436 OPS against southpaws this season — ripped a hit through the right side of the infield, giving the Yankees a lead they only padded from there.
Wells added a second single off a lefty — Alec Gamboa in the seventh inning, plus a sacrifice fly in the eighth against Brayan Bello — to make it two hits off southpaws in the postseason, which is remarkable for a player who had 11 hits (in 99 plate appearances) against such pitching all season.
“I think just overall I’m feeling better, seeing the ball well and just competing up there,” said Wells, who has been a different hitter since a stint on the injured list in June with cervical headaches.
Those 15 days sidelined, when he could heal, refresh his mind and tweak his swing, may have saved his job and Yankees future.
“In the moment, [I] didn’t realize how much it was affecting me,” Wells said of the headaches, “but taking the time and getting back and feeling healthy, I feel like I can see the ball a lot better.”
He felt better on the other side of the injured list, but the results did not arrive immediately. And his inability against pitching of all types through the middle of July ensured the Yankees at least tested the trade market. He was hitting .152 with a .501 OPS on July 19. As much as they valued his rapport with pitchers and his defense, he had nearly become unplayable.
And yet Wells kept playing, made steady progress and showed enough in late July and early August to dissuade Cashman from overpaying in prospects.

At a time when catchers typically are wearing down, in August and September, Wells posted his two best months of the year.
And even though the date read Sept. 29, he showed Tuesday why October may further his revival.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman is expected to be busy this winter. While the Bronx Bombers are set to begin their playoff push after winning 93 games in 2026, the roster could certainly improve. Third base is a clear area for Cashman to target in the offseason. Catcher and center field are also positions to keep an eye on.
Nevertheless, the Yankees could soon have a massive hole at second base as well. Jazz Chisholm is set to become an unrestricted free agent after his one-year, $10.2 million deal ends. A continued partnership between the two-time All-Star and New York was previously considered a no-brainer. In fact, the Yankees were once predicted to give Chisholm a $300 million extension. This, however, now seems increasingly unlikely.
Bleacher Report’s Zach Buckley is now anticipating that New York will sign fellow second baseman Brandon Lowe this winter. The current Pittsburgh Pirates infielder is expected to be one of the top players at his position in free agency and is not expected to re-sign with his current club. According to the reporter, the Yankees should be able to land Lowe on a three-year contract.
This is not the first time that Buckley has linked the New York Yankees to Lowe. The writer previously claimed that Cashman will soon replace Chisholm with the Pirates star. Buckley even predicted that the second baseman could get at least $25 million per year in his next deal. If true, the Yankees will be rewarding the infielder with a $75 million contract in the coming months.
New York Yankees Will Face Heavy Competition to Sign Brandon Lowe
Assuming the New York Yankees sign Lowe, it would seemingly be an upgrade at the position. The Pirates infielder currently beats Chisholm in practically every offensive category. In fact, stolen bases are the only significant area where the Yankees star has the edge. Lowe, on the other hand, is slashing an impressive .260/.331/.493 in Pittsburgh this season.
He led all Major League Baseball second basemen in home runs, slugging, and OPS on the campaign as well. Lowe’s 5.4 WAR was also tops among players at his position in 2026. Overall, this particular figure was tied for 15th-best in all of baseball. In fact, the second baseman’s WAR was only slightly lower than other stars such as Junior Caminero, Randy Arozarena, and Elly De La Cruz.
The New York Yankees, however, will face tough competition in the Lowe sweepstakes. As Buckley points out, several MLB teams will want to sign the star in free agency. The Toronto Blue Jays have already been linked with a potential move for the infielder as well.
New York Set to Host Rivals in Postseason Clash
For now, the New York Yankees will focus on the 2026 playoffs. The club is set to host the Boston Red Sox in the wild card round. The two rivals will begin the five-game series in the Bronx on September 29. New York recently named Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Gerrit Cole as starting pitchers for the first three games. Immediately following the campaign, however, Cashman will look to free agency to strengthen his roster.
