The thing about chasing an object is that if it matches your speed, there is really nothing you can do. The New York Yankees learned this hard lesson down the stretch when any goals they had of running down the Rays to at least make it a competitive fight down the stretch fell flat — not because the Yankees underwhelmed in the final month of the season. In fact, one could hardly ask for more out of this team given the obstacles it had to face as the Rays left nothing to chance. Despite winning 15 of 23 games in September, the Yankees couldn't gain a game on the Rays, who won 16 of 24 to wrap up their season.
What looked like the likeliest scenario for quite some time now, given the state of the other two divisions in the American League, has come to pass. The Yankees, who are the second-best team in the AL, will have to go through the most difficult of schedules to make it out of their league for the second time in the past three seasons. A three-game Wild Card round against the feisty Boston Red Sox and all the potential pitfalls a short series can bring await—one with a feeling of déjà vu, happening for the second straight season. Then, if they make it out, it's a date with the Rays while the AL Central and AL West clubs battle it out on the inferior side of the bracket.
It hasn't been the smoothest ride to get to this point, and based on how Brian Cashman has polled all year long, it's safe to say expectations were not met — even if there are obvious caveats beyond his control as to why the Yankees are exactly where they are. Early in the season, when Cashman polled at 41 percent, the Yankees were battling with the Rays for the AL East title — but if you polled most fans, you would've been hard-pressed to find many who bought the Rays as a 99-win team. Frankly, there are probably those who, even now, don't buy them at that level even now, but that's an entirely separate conversation to have in the analysis of the gap between these two clubs, particularly at full strength. Cashman's approval rating nosedived as did the Yankees' chances of winning this division, partially due to questionable moves but overwhelmingly due to absences that all the money in the world couldn't plan for.
For three months between June and August, the Yankees put up a wRC+ below league average, clearly struggling in the absence of the best hitter in the sport. The deadline acquisition of Luis Garcia Jr. in particular gave the offense a boost as he delivered an .842 OPS in August — even that wasn't enough to take the team's line over 100, coming in with a 96 wRC+ for the month.
In September, though, the offense came through with a 104 wRC+ that may not seem like much, but with this team's rotation, it's how you go about winning 15 of 23 games. All of this after starting off the month with the bad news of yet another Trent Grisham hamstring injury, this one keeping him out for the rest of the regular season. Spencer Jones continues to defy the laws of what can be described as sensible production coming with obscene strikeout rates, with a 110 wRC+ on the month despite a strikeout rate above 38 percent.
While Aaron Judge's brief return before getting injured again helps, this September improvement boils down primarily to the work of Ben Rice, who, after a disappointing summer — given the high bar he set for himself — came alive in a big way. Still, if you're wondering about the changes in impact from Rice with and without a fully stocked lineup, the Yankees first baseman delivered 21 RBI with seven homers in 24 games in May. The same Rice then hit six homers in 22 games this past month and only drove in 11. Those 11 RBI did not lead the team, with the distinction left to George Lombard Jr., who drove in 16 with five homers, providing more power than he had in the previous month. Back to the deadline acquisitions, though, as Garcia cooled off, Heliot Ramos finally showed up, proving a worthy presence in the lineup, specifically against left-handed pitchers.
It was business as usual for this ultra-talented staff, with Cam Schlittler wrapping up a likely Cy Young campaign with yet another sub-2.00 ERA month. Carlos Rodón was nearly as dominant as Schlittler, with both kind of showing up Max Fried, who had a solid September, and, lastly, Will Warren impressing; the only one who had more than his fair share of issues was Gerrit Cole. But looking forward to the Wild Card round in which he'll start the third game, if needed, Cole impressed in his final regular-season start against the Rays.
About the Wild Card round, the Yankees already announced their starters versus Boston, with Schlittler going in game 1, followed by Fried and lastly Cole. While Boston hasn't officially announced their starters, expectations are that Sonny Gray, the AL leader in wins this season with 18, will take the ball for Game 1 and likely be followed by left-hander Payton Tolle.
When it comes to transactions, not a lot stood out. With a plethora of utility options, the Yankees chose to designate Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment when they had to open up a 40-man spot for Clarke Schmidt. Cabrera was picked up by the Reds and was one of two players to leave the Yankees this month, alongside righty Chase Hampton — picked up by the Nats (and recently discarded) after being DFA'd early in the month. Hampton didn't appear in the bigs for the Yankees.
It's a simple yet loaded question whether you approve of Cashman's job in September, depending on how much emphasis you want to give to certain merits and demerits in how the Yankees have been managed this season. In many ways, the déjà vu doesn't come strictly from a playoff series against the Red Sox. It's more so from yet another second-place finish in the AL East against a team widely regarded as inferior to the Yankees before the start of the season.
So with the regular season officially over and the playoffs immediately ahead, do you approve of Brian Cashman? As always, there's a lot to factor into a "yes" or a "no," and you might feel like your answer is more of a soft "yes" or "no" than a stamp of approval or a sharp rebuke. However, the binary question is the best way to get a direct read on fans' thoughts.

New York Yankees general manager Brian Cashman spent the 2026 trade deadline adding offense. With Aaron Judge still out and Giancarlo Stanton permanently MIA, it made some sense on paper to add bats like Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos.
You know what didn't make sense? Walking away from the deadline without a single pitching addition. And yet, that's exactly what Cashman did. For whatever reason, Cashman deemed that the market wasn't right to add reliever depth, despite the fact that the Yankees have been running arms like Brent Headrick and Fernando Cruz into the ground all season long.
Not surprisingly, Headrick is beginning to show signs of fatigue (he is human, after all), and Cruz is now injured. The Yankees are signing no-name arms to stay afloat, and Cashman deserves blame for this situation. At least New York Post's Joel Sherman is seeing things clearly.
Brian Cashman thought he could get away with Yankees current bullpen
Are Yankees really still hoping that arms like the untrustworthy Luis Gil or the recovering Clarke Schmidt will help make this crisis go away? That's where we're at entering October, and it's sad.
This roster has a ton of talent, and the American League is decidedly weak this season. But since Cashman ignored the pitching staff at the deadline, their World Series chances have no doubt taken a hit.
While the overachieving Tampa Bay Rays held off the Yankees and Red Sox, and New York deserves credit for emerging from the "grave danger zone" of losing ground to Boston, this front office oversight still doomed them to the Wild Card. Cruz's injury alone doesn't prove this, by the way — he'd been awful since the All-Star break. Anyone watching the Yankees has been able to see that their bullpen has slowly been breaking down. It was happening way before the deadline! It's a miracle things aren't much worse.
Fans can't be too shocked at Cashman's performance (or lack thereof). This has become an annual tradition. He makes false assumptions that the Yankees have enough depth in a certain area (oftentimes the pitching staff), and they never do. He hates purchasing insurance, despite evidence to the contrary that this team underachieves in August (almost every year) and enters the playoffs wounded and tired.
Getting to the postseason has never been a problem for the Yankees during the Cashman era. It's the whole advancing once they get there that's been consistently disappointing, and you can trace that back to Cashman's deadline every season.
Max Fried came back earlier than expected. Great! Schmidt vacillated between being close and injured. Splendid! None of that changes the fact that Cashman should have added reinforcements at the deadline and failed to do so. The script is so familiar at this point. Fans just want something different for once.

CC Sabathia vio muchas ceremonias en honor a exjugadores durante 11 temporadas con los Yankees de Nueva York y nunca imaginó que él sería uno de los homenajeados.
Sabathia se convirtió el viernes en el 24.º jugador o mánager en ver retirado su número, y el zurdo miembro del Salón de la Fama fue homenajeado con una placa en Monument Park durante una ceremonia previa al primer juego de una doble cartelera contra Baltimore.
Sabathia se unió a Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera, Andy Pettitte y Jorge Posada como el quinto integrante de los Yankees campeones de la Serie Mundial de 2009 con un número retirado y una placa.
"Nunca me imaginé entrando a Monument Park y creo que esa fue la razón por la que tenía tanto miedo de venir aquí, porque uno nunca piensa que va a ganarse a la afición de los Yankees o a la ciudad. Así que poder estar sentado aquí ahora, haber jugado aquí 11 años, es una sensación increíble, y por eso he dicho en las últimas semanas que esto se siente más grande para mí que el Salón de la Fama, porque sé lo que estaba en juego cuando vine aquí”, señaló Sabathia.
Con 46 años, Sabathia firmó un contrato de 161 millones de dólares por siete años antes de la temporada 2009, después de que el gerente general Brian Cashman lo convenciera tras una reunión inicial en diciembre de 2008. El contrato fue el más grande en ese momento para un lanzador agente libre.
Sabathia tuvo marca de 19-8 con efectividad de 3,37 en 34 aperturas con los Yankees en su primera temporada. Ganó el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana, con marca de 2-0 y efectividad de 1,13 en una victoria en seis juegos sobre los Angelinos de Los Ángeles, y abrió los Juegos 1 y 4 cuando los Yankees vencieron a Filadelfia para conquistar su 27.º título.
Sabathia terminó con marca de 251-161, efectividad de 3,74 y 3.093 ponches —tercero entre los zurdos detrás de Randy Johnson y Steve Carlton— durante 19 temporadas con Cleveland (2001-08), Milwaukee (2008) y los Yankees (2009-19).
Durante 11 temporadas en Nueva York, Sabathia tuvo marca de 134-88 con efectividad de 3,81 y 1.700 ponches. Ocupa el cuarto lugar en la historia de la franquicia en ponches, el séptimo en aperturas, el décimo en victorias y el 11.º en entradas lanzadas.
Sabathia fue elegido al Salón de la Fama en su primera aparición en la boleta en 2025, al recibir el 86,8% de los votos. Fue exaltado junto con Billy Wagner e Ichiro Suzuki, excompañero suyo en los Yankees de 2012 a 2014.
“Esa ceremonia fue increíble, surrealista. Estaba diciendo allá afuera que tengo tantos compañeros famosos, ya sea Mo, Derek, Andy. Así que he estado en la ceremonia muchas veces, pero que esa ceremonia fuera para mí es especial, y que mi familia estuviera ahí fue genial”, comentó Sabathia.
La ceremonia de los Yankees comenzó con mensajes en video de Jeter, Paul O’Neill, Jorge Posada y Bernie Williams, y Sabathia develó la placa junto con su esposa Amber, dos de sus hijos, dos amigos y su madre, Margie.
Después de los momentos destacados en video, Sabathia saludó a los aficionados desde un carrito de golf a lo largo de la pista de advertencia. Recibió un saco azul, una versión enmarcada de su placa y del número retirado, además de un anillo conmemorativo de su carrera, de manos del gerente general Brian Cashman, quien fue abucheado por los aficionados.
Tras la ceremonia, Sabathia realizó el lanzamiento ceremonial de la primera bola a su hijo Carsten, primera base de ligas menores de Milwaukee.

NUEVA YORK — CC Sabathia presenció muchas ceremonias en honor a exjugadores durante sus 11 temporadas con los Yankees de Nueva York y nunca imaginó que él sería uno de los homenajeados.
Sabathia se convirtió en el vigésimo cuarto jugador o entrenador en ver retirado su número, y el lanzador zurdo miembro del Salón de la Fama fue homenajeado con una placa en Monument Park durante una ceremonia previa al primer partido de una doble jornada contra Baltimore el viernes.
Sabathia se unió a Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera, Andy Pettitte y Jorge Posada como el quinto miembro de los Yankees campeones de la Serie Mundial de 2009 en tener un número y una placa retirados.
“Nunca me imaginé entrando al Monument Park y creo que esa fue la razón por la que tenía tanto miedo de venir aquí, porque uno nunca piensa que va a ganarse a los fanáticos de los Yankees ni a la ciudad”, dijo Sabathia. “Así que poder estar aquí ahora, después de jugar aquí durante 11 años, es una sensación increíble, y por eso he dicho en las últimas semanas que esto es más importante para mí que el Salón de la Fama, porque sé lo que estaba en juego cuando llegué aquí”.
Sabathia, que ahora tiene 46 años, firmó un contrato de 161 millones de dólares por siete años antes de la temporada 2009, tras ser convencido por el gerente general Brian Cashman después de una reunión inicial en diciembre de 2008. En aquel momento, fue el contrato más cuantioso para un lanzador agente libre.
Sabathia tuvo una marca de 19-8 con una efectividad de 3.37 en 34 aperturas con los Yankees en su primera temporada. Ganó el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana, con una marca de 2-0 y una efectividad de 1.13 en una victoria de seis juegos sobre los Angelinos de Los Ángeles, y fue abridor en los Juegos 1 y 4 cuando los Yankees vencieron a Filadelfia para obtener su 27º título.
Sabathia tuvo un récord de 251-161 con una efectividad de 3.74 y 3,093 ponches, tercero entre los lanzadores zurdos detrás de Randy Johnson y Steve Carlton, durante 19 temporadas con Cleveland (2001-08), Milwaukee (2008) y los Yankees (2009-19).
Durante sus 11 temporadas en Nueva York, Sabathia registró un récord de 134 victorias y 88 derrotas, con una efectividad de 3.81 y 1700 ponches. Ocupa el cuarto lugar en la historia de la franquicia en ponches, el séptimo en aperturas, el décimo en victorias y el undécimo en entradas lanzadas.
Sabathia fue elegido para el Salón de la Fama en su primer año de elegibilidad en 2025, recibiendo el 86,8% de los votos. Fue incorporado junto con Billy Wagner e Ichiro Suzuki, excompañero de los Yankees entre 2012 y 2014.
“Esa ceremonia fue increíble, surrealista”, dijo Sabathia. “Estaba comentando que tengo muchos compañeros famosos, como Mo, Derek y Andy. He asistido a la ceremonia muchas veces, pero que esta fuera solo para mí es especial, y tener a mi familia allí fue genial”.
La ceremonia de los Yankees comenzó con mensajes en vídeo de Jeter, Paul O'Neill, Jorge Posada y Bernie Williams, y Sabathia develó la placa junto a su esposa Amber, dos de sus hijos, dos amigos y su madre, Margie.
Tras la proyección de un vídeo con los mejores momentos, Sabathia saludó a los aficionados desde un carrito de golf junto a la pista de advertencia. When the New York Yankees looked to shore up their bullpen last season, GM Brian Cashman knew that it wouldn’t come cheaply. The Yankees were ready to part ways with talented prospects if it meant a better chance at improving the ball club, and it has mostly paid off. After they made a deal with the Pittsburgh Pirates for pitcher David Bednar, some critics actually thought that the Yankees got away with highway robbery. But as it turns out, that trade was a win-win for both sides. And that's mainly because of Rafael Flores Jr.
Despite missing out on the playoffs in 2026, the Pittsburgh Pirates have had one of their best seasons in years. They even have an opportunity to finish over the .500 mark for the first time since the 2018 season. That success has largely been fueled by offensive breakout seasons from players like Flores Jr.
The young catcher has put the league on notice with an impressive stretch to close out the season. After hitting just four home runs in 65 games for Triple-A Indianapolis, Flores Jr. has gone on an absolute tear for the Pirates. In 43 games in the big leagues, he's launched 10 bombs and driven in 22 runs. His .910 OPS for the Buccos is also more than 200 points higher than his season mark in the minors.
For a Yankees club that has been severely lacking offensive production from the catcher position, it certainly stings to see yet another former player catch fire for another team. Similar to the season that Carlos Narváez had for the Boston Red Sox in 2024, Flores Jr. may be giving the Yankees a bit of seller's remorse. We will have to wait and see if Flores Jr. will be able to keep up his hot bat next season, but as of now, it appears that the Bednar trade has become about as even as it gets.
The Yankees needed David Bednar at any cost
Seeing Flores Jr. flourish in Pittsburgh is like seeing an ex become a millionaire overnight. You can't help but feel a little jealous at the type of season he's had while Austin Wells and Ali Sánchez struggle to supply any production at the plate. In a third of the games played, Flores Jr. has all but matched the fWAR of both Wells and Sánchez combined in 2026. The former highly-rated Yankees prospect is swiftly matching the hype.
Regardless of the price that they paid, Bednar has been an amazing pickup for the Yankees. In a season and a half, he’s collected 44 saves and his presence has really helped to stabilize the back end of the bullpen. His ability to routinely collect more than three outs in any game adds a level of versatility that eludes even some of the most elite closers.
In his 83 appearances for the Yankees over the last two seasons, Bednar boasts an ERA+ of 170 and a very respectable 1.011 WHIP. While he can sometimes flirt with danger and make ball games interesting, he has been as close to a sure thing to pick up a save as the Yankees have had in years.
Although his 1.9 fWAR doesn’t quite rank him among some of the 10 best relievers in baseball, the value he has brought to the Yankees is unmistakable. That means that he was worth the price that the Yankees paid to acquire him, even if the trade appears en route to becoming more balanced over time.
Good pitching will always be key for any team to win a championship. Preventing the other team from putting up crooked numbers is one of the most effective ways to come out on top at the end of a game. But it can be difficult to find and develop the level of pitching needed to achieve that. This can be especially true when it comes to late-inning relievers. That means a premium is usually paid.
We’ve seen the Yankees win and lose trades over the years. It's all part of the risk you take when you build a win-now team. Some of those trades hit, some don't. The Yankees needed a pitcher like Bednar to help them in the postseason so they pulled the trigger. And while trading Flores Jr. for that reason could benefit the Pirates more in the long run, a World Series title in 2026 would erase any feeling of regret for the Yankees.

The New York Yankees split a doubleheader with the first-place Tampa Bay Rays on Tuesday, winning the first game 2-0 behind eight shutout innings from Carlos Rodón and the 35th save of the season by closer David Bednar.
By losing the second game 6-1, however, the Yankees were eliminated from the race for the American League East pennant, and the Rays clinched it. The Yankees are now locked into the AL’s top Wild Card spot, and will most likely face the Boston Red Sox in a best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium starting Sept. 29.
With the regular season winding down, the Yankees’ front office now must decide what to do with Bednar, who played a key role in the Yankees’ run to the postseason but becomes eligible for free agency when the signing period opens on Nov. 5.
Bednar recorded the second-best save total of his career, but the achievement hasn’t yet earned him a contract commitment from Yankees general manager Brian Cashman.
With the bullpen thin on proven arms and October now locked in, letting a closer walk to the open market without so much as an extension conversation raises questions about who closes games for New York after this year.
Bednar Built an Unlikely Path to Closer Duty
David Jeffrey Bednar was born Oct. 10, 1994, in Pittsburgh and grew up nearby in Mars, Pennsylvania. San Diego took the 6-foot-1, 250-pound right-hander in the 35th round of the 2016 draft out of Lafayette College, hardly the pedigree of a future big-league closer.
Bednar debuted with the Padres on Sept. 1, 2019, then landed in Pittsburgh a little more than a year later as part of a three-team trade involving the Mets. He turned that opportunity into back-to-back All-Star nods and a league-leading 39 saves in 2023, becoming the closer in a rebuilding Pirates bullpen.
A rocky 2024 and a brief demotion to Triple-A in 2025 threatened to derail that run, but New York bet on a bounce-back. The Yankees acquired the two-time All-Star reliever on July 31, 2025, sending Pittsburgh minor-league catchers Rafael Flores and Edgleen Pérez and outfielder Brian Sánchez in return. Bednar answered by posting a 2.19 ERA with 10 saves in 22 games down the stretch in 2025.
Yankees Weigh Bednar’s Free Agency Future
Bednar signed a one-year, $9 million contract in January to avoid arbitration, his final season of club control before hitting the open market. He’s made good on it, posting a 2.54 ERA and 35 saves through 62 appearances this season, the second-highest total of his career behind his 39-save 2023 campaign, with 74 strikeouts over 67 1/3 innings.
Bednar carries a 1.83 ERA over his last 30 outings, a run interrupted only by a Sept. 16 blown save at Minnesota in which both runs he allowed were unearned.
Speculation surfaced in June that Bednar could be predicted to lose the closer role to Fernando Cruz, but he held the job through the stretch run regardless.
No extension talks have surfaced publicly. Bleacher Report‘s Joel Reuter called Bednar one of the most reliable closers in baseball and floated a hypothetical three-year, $45 million deal as a “top priority” reunion. MLB Trade Rumors, which included Bednar on its list of 2026-27 MLB free agents, gave him only an honorable mention on its rankings of the winter’s top relievers.
Bednar should be eligible for a qualifying offer, having spent the entire 2026 season with New York and never having received one before. The amount of the MLB qualifying offer is estimated to be set at a projected $23.1 million this offseason, though relievers rarely draw the tag at that price since multiyear closer deals typically land below it.

The Tampa Bay Rays come to town today for four games in three days. There's a mid-50s chill in the air. Every step you take alternates between dewy grass and dry leaves. It's October baseball, baby.
Except, because of the way the standings are situated, the Yankees will likely need to win at least one playoff game to even reach the actual month of October. One Rays win out of four games this week sentences the Yankees to the Wild Card round against the Red Sox, taking place Sept. 29-Oct. 1. That's not how it was supposed to be, but that's how it is.
Do you rage at the sky? The Yankees went through a 5-15 stretch midsummer, then steered out of it nicely, playing some of the best ball in the league in August and September without their Captain. But the Rays were still better. Every time the Yankees won, seemingly so did the Rays. Ditto for losses. They synced their inanity pretty nicely with one another. At one point, the Rays hit a game-tying home run with two outs in the ninth off Mason Miller that was in a Padre's glove and was dropped over the fence. Do you tip your cap, or does the Rays' relentlessness make you angrier?
Aaron Boone, Brian Cashman to blame for Yankees' Wild Card reality?
Do you blame Aaron Boone? The best argument for ditching him with an underwhelming playoff finish is the same as it's always been for me: Time for a new voice. Something has to change. The other arguments ring kind of hollow this year, to be honest. He's manned the ship during a season where injuries should've killed the Yankees, not just derailed them from the pursuit of their primary goal of winning the AL East, but didn't at all. He's done a fantastic job managing an undermanned bullpen.
Do we blame the man who gave him the undermanned bullpen? I lean more in that direction. Brian Cashman's hubris led him to believe the waiver wire and his surplus of injured starting pitchers would build a better bullpen than what was available all offseason/at the trade deadline. We'll see if he's right, but he already failed to account for August wear-and-tear. He crowded the DH room with purpose, forcing Aaron Judge back into right field, then back onto the IL. We needed bats. We didn't necessarily need an added logjam of non-fielders.
Unless the Yankees can somehow sweep a four-game series, including a doubleheader, this week, the Rays will celebrate on their turf. Will it motivate them more than it motivates you, the general fan, some of whom have already counted them out? It had better. Leaving this series with a bad taste in their mouths could pay dividends. It could also end their season before October begins.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees opted not to add any relief pitchers at the MLB trade deadline. Why? Because Ryan Weathers was going to end up in the bullpen, and Clarke Schmidt was due to return.
The Yankees were relying on two pitchers with extensive injury histories to solidify their bullpen in October. What could possibly go wrong?
Well, everything that could have gone wrong has gone wrong for New York.
Weathers suffered an elbow flexor strain last month and has been sidelined ever since. It now doesn't appear that the left-hander will return before the playoffs, leaving his postseason status in jeopardy.
Schmidt? He suffered a setback at the beginning of August due to forearm cramping. He then finally returned last week and pitched all of one game before ultimately succumbing to biceps cramping while warming up in the bullpen over the weekend.
Naturally, New York ruled him out for the contest.
Schmidt said it was precautionary and that he didn't want to push through, but are we really to think that a pitcher who had been sidelined since last summer after undergoing Tommy John surgery and had made a grand total of 30 appearances between 2024 and 2025 is going to magically rebound and be just fine?
Maybe the right-hander really is okay and will be available sooner than we think, but you can't help but feel that Schmidt's playoff status, much like that of Weathers, is now in limbo.
It make Brian Cashman's mind-boggling decision not to acquire relief help last month that much more egregious, and it moves the Yankees even further away from a deep October run, something that was probably already foreign anyway following Aaron Judge's latest trip to the injured list.
Yes, New York picked up John Schreiber on the waiver wire, and he has certainly helped, logging a 2.00 ERA over eight relief appearances. He will almost certainly be on the postseason roster.
But Schreiber alone isn't enough. Not with Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn burning the candle from both ends and Tim Hill turning into a batting practice machine.
Had Weathers and Schmidt remained healthy, there's no question they would have been able to help. It's the fact that Cashman was whimsically relying on it that's so nonsensical.
I've been a big Cashman defender over the years. I think he's been a very good general manager for a long time. But it's becoming harder and harder to defend his decisions.
Just about every other contending team acquired bullpen help at the trade deadline. Apparently, the Yankees were the only ballclub too good to do so.

We know what you’re thinking: The New York Yankees cannot realistically replace Aaron Judge.
Unfortunately for Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman, they have no choice. Judge landed back on the injured list with a right calf strain, and the earliest that he could return is next Sunday’s regular-season finale against the Orioles. The Yankees have not committed to the three-time AL MVP potentially being ready for the AL Wild Card Series.
“I usually deal with calf stuff all year long,” Judge told reporters on Saturday. “It usually doesn’t get to [the media], and I usually don’t miss any games. So that was kind of the same thing I was feeling. I was working my way back, and then something kind of grabs you at a strange time.”
So, who will man right field in Judge’s absence? Will it be Spencer Jones, who has flashed as a rookie? What about Cody Bellinger, who could shift over from left field?
As it turns out, the answer might be speedy utilityman José Caballero. Seriously.
José Caballero could start in the Yankees’ outfield following Aaron Judge’s latest injury
The 30-year-old Caballero drew the start in center field on Saturday night, hitting two singles and drawing the walk in a 5-3 loss. He's played 20 of his 130 games in the outfield, with most of that action coming in the corner spots.
For what it’s worth, we’ve always liked Caballero enough that we repeatedly advocated for the Yankees to consider naming him the full-time shortstop and trading Anthony Volpe. So we’re not opposed to the thought of him playing right, with Bellinger starting in center and Heliot Ramos taking over in left field.
The 5-foot-9, 190-pound Caballero's calling card has always been his legs, and he's stolen at least 26 bases in each of his first four seasons. This year has been no exception, with him swiping a team-leading 32 bases in 43 attempts. But to his credit, Caballero has added some power to his game, recording a career-high 14 home runs in nearly 450 plate appearances.
Bellinger has played 118 of his 127 games in left field, though he has extensive experience in both center and right. The reigning All-Star Game MVP is also one of the Yankees' most reliable hitters, even as his OPS has dropped from .813 to .781.
Objectively speaking, the Yankees can afford to have an outfield consisting of Caballero, Bellinger, and either Ramos or Jones. Trent Grisham remains out with a right hamstring problem, though Boone has hinted they’d get the two-time Gold Glove winner back in time for the playoffs. As things stand, the Yankees would host the rival Red Sox in a first-round rematch of last year’s Wild Card Series.
Ideally for the Yankees, they’ll have Judge batting second and playing right field next Tuesday night. But if you’re looking for a dark horse candidate to shine this postseason, you could do far worse than the versatile Caballero.

More than almost any other New York Yankees playoff run, this October's edition will provide either immediate vindication for Brian Cashman's trade deadline strategy or all-new reasons to directly blame him for the team's failure. It should be fascinating to watch, if you don't actually have much emotional energy invested in the team's well-being. Clarke Schmidt's postgame note on Sunday evening was just another reason to be anxious about the way this bullpen was constructed and the amount of variables therein.
Trade deadline predictions for the Yankees' haul this year were astoundingly easy to make. A catcher, first and foremost. An impact bat, that was obvious. And then two bullpen arms to help save their late-inning core from running aground before the year ended. Maybe one would be a certified ace, a tier below Mason Miller, but still devilish. Maybe another would be a bounce back candidate or a never-was, someone who Matt Blake could unearth. Either way, the choices were many, but the outcome was obvious: CashGod would be trading for some relievers. Plural.
But then the deadline came and went. We weren't disappointed by the quality of the haul, but rather in a whole new way. No catcher? No relievers? Was this a mistake? Is the deadline tomorrow?
Nope. Cashman went all in and decided that either the prices were too high or not commensurate with the talent available. Instead, he would look the other way and ignore the rising cost of wear-and-tear in August and piece together some bullpen reinforcements using alternate levers. The waiver wire became his friend. His rotation became a plucking ground, as did his own Injured List. Will Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Weathers, Luis Gil, Will Warren, John Schreiber and Michael Fulmer be more valuable together than any names he could've added on Aug. 3? That's the bet. We'll see. I have my doubts, but he has his agenda.
And, in case you weren't already lacking confidence, Schmidt's bicep barked on Sunday and prevented him from entering the game, a game that ace reliever Brent Headrick lit on fire with an average fastball that dipped about a mile and a half below his standard velocity on the season. Hmm. If only he could've been rested during the dog days of summer.
Clarke Schmidt's worrisome postgame comments, Brent Headrick outing vs. Diamondbacks tell the same Yankees story
So, for the record, that's Schmidt - after one MLB outing this year - admitting that, out of precaution, he stopped warming up when his arm barked. His rehab was also halted along the way when he felt forearm cramping on Aug. 4, just one day post-trade deadline. The Yankees getting him back to the MLB level after a summer 2025 Tommy John surgery is remarkable. This is not someone a team should be relying on to cover meaningful postseason innings. And yet.
Headrick's stumble comes in an otherwise phenomenal year, and even as he's lost some gas down the stretch, he's still managed to mostly make things work. He's an expert at limiting inherited runners from scoring, and he's alternated spotless outings with troublesome ones post-deadline. No one knows for certain whether bringing on an experienced seventh-inning guy or two in early August would've prevented the effects of overuse from piling up on Headrick's left arm, but we do know having a viable alternative now could help them deemphasize Headrick if he's struggling to recapture his former glory. Batters hit .345 off him in 15 August games.
That group of alternatives probably doesn't, or shouldn't, include Schmidt, who's hanging on by a thread. Again, it'll be Cashman's crew - Schreiber, Fulmer, Warren, and maybe Weathers, who won't be rehabbing in a regular season game - vs. the field to see who's better equipped for October. Fascinating, if it weren't so presumptuous.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees fans are frustrated. It's been 17 long years since they've enjoyed a parade down the Canyon of Heroes following a World Series victory. The man primarily responsible for that frustration is general manager Brian Cashman.
If you ask veteran MLB insider Ken Rosenthal, though, Cashman is doing a bang-up job. Rosenthal gushed about Cashman during a recent appearance on Foul Territory.
"It's time, it's past time, to understand what [Brian] Cashman has accomplished," Rosenthal said. "And all of those years finishing above .500, since 1998, yes, they have had financial advantages, too. So have a lot of other teams. No other team has had a winning record every year.
"Now I know, certain fans, certain Yankees fans, will say, 'No World Series title since 2009.' Yes, that is true. It's undeniable, and some of the teams have not been constructed as well as they could've been. I would expect Cashman would say that as well. However, they are always in the mix."
He went on to acknowledge what the standard is in New York - World Series or bust - and he detailed that through line from George Steinbrenner to Derek Jeter to Aaron Judge. But ultimately, his point was that the playoffs are random and that Cashman shouldn't be held accountable for not winning a ring since 2009. Regular season greatness, in Rosenthal's opinion, is a better measuring stick of a GM's abilities.
Sounds ridiculous, right? Even if we grant him that the World Series is tough to win, and it is, that's the point! We're still looking at a clear decline. Think back to the dynasty that began in 1996. The Yankees won four World Series, yes, but they had also lost two others (2001, 2003), meaning that during an eight-year stretch they made it to the final showdown six times. Now consider that since 2009 they only have one World Series appearance to their credit: the 2024 defeat at the hands of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
It's hard not to see a distinct break. Remember, too, that Cashman ascended to the role of general manager on February 3, 1998. He's not fully responsible for those championship clubs, as they had been molded and shaped by Gene Michael and Bob Watson before him.
Also remember that during the 2008-2009 offseason, Cashman's seat was scorching hot, and he was basically mandated by George to go on the huge spending spree that netted New York CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira, and A.J. Burnett. If his hand hadn't been forced, we likely wouldn't have seen those splashes, and we don't have the ring to show for it.
An honest assessment of Brian Cashman's Yankees tenure pegs him as a middle-of-the-pack general manager
Going back to Rosenthal for a second, he's also been on an apology tour for Cincinnati Reds president of baseball operations, Nick Krall. Krall runs a small-market team, but he enjoys having an MVP-caliber player in Elly De La Cruz, a young ace in Chase Burns, and the likely NL Rookie of the Year in Sal Stewart on pre-arb contracts. That trio makes up just under $2.5 million of Cincinnati's $133 million payroll. He could've set the remaining $130 million on fire and gotten better results.
I bring this up as a reminder that insiders like Rosenthal's sole job is to get inside information and break stories. They get that by cultivating relationships, so when you hear them give an edgy or unconventional opinion, it's because they don't want to hurt a source's feelings.
This isn't to say that Cashman is a bad GM. He's made his share of great moves. He's made blockbuster trades like acquiring Alex Rodriguez, Giancarlo Stanton, and Juan Soto. He's found diamonds in the rough like Brent Headrick (and several others).
But the issue with Cashman is that he doesn't learn from his past mistakes. After failing to acquire prime Johan Santana to protect Phil Hughes, Joba Chamberlain, and Ian Kennedy, he let Ivan Nova, Eduardo Nunez, and Adam Warren stand in the way of trading for Cliff Lee a few years later. Then he compounded the mistake when he failed to sign Lee the following offseason.
In recent years, he's failed to capitalize on Aaron Judge being the literal reincarnation of Babe Ruth by shying away from emptying out the farm to acquire difference makers who would have changed the Yankees' calculus.
It's impossible to look at his missteps and not see titles left on the table. It's criminal that he's enjoyed the best hitter this generation has produced, yet since 2017 has just one World Series appearance to show for it.
Go back to the 1998 team. That should have been his lesson. That club laid waste to the American League, winning 114 games. Entering October, a World Series berth felt inevitable. Going into the World Series against the San Diego Padres, the only question was whether the Yankees would hoist the Commissioner's Trophy after four games or five.
Since those glory days, winning the division is no longer a guarantee. Making the playoffs has sometimes felt like it's on shaky ground. The standard has been lowered, but by the organization, not the fans.

item.content:encoded:
For the last several months, Brian Cashman has kept a close eye on his assistant director of baseball operations. Any lavish purchase — a luxury car, a swanky penthouse, fancy new clothes — would be an indication that Mike Pinsky had come into life-changing money, the Yankees’ general manager figured.
“If he’s driving a Lamborghini, then I know he won,” Cashman said, referring to Pinsky’s casting on Season 51 of “Survivor.”
The 33-year-old will make his debut on the CBS reality show on Wednesday. It is a “lifelong dream” come true for Pinsky, who grew up a superfan of the franchise before traveling to Fiji’s Mamanuca Islands to film between April and May this year.
“I spend all day, every day, sort of evaluating players from the comfort of a stadium seat or my desk chair, and inside of me is this burning passion to actually be the one competing myself,” said Pinsky, who began watching “Survivor” when he was 8, created his own version of the game with his friends, and even worked one of the show’s catchphrases into his marriage proposal. “I long to actually be the one playing the game, and so this was a really interesting opportunity to actually get to be the player instead of the evaluator, and actually see what I’m made of.”
Pinsky added that he brought the Yankees’ championship-or-bust mindset with him to Fiji.
“Anytime you’re playing a game, anytime you’re competing, you play to win,” he said. “So I don’t do anything for second place.”
As per his agreement with CBS, Pinsky could not disclose how he fared on the show, or much of anything that happened during filming. That has not stopped Cashman and the rest of the Yankees’ baseball ops department from trying to find out, though.
“We’ve been peppering him and teasing him and trying to steal information,” Cashman said. “He’s like Fort Knox.”
Pinsky did say that Cashman, Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner and the rest of his colleagues were “incredibly gracious” and supportive of him being on the show.
Filming required Pinsky to be away from the Yankees and cut off from the outside world for an unspecified period of time at the beginning of the season, so he needed permission to leave his job. Luckily for him, that “was probably the most opportune time,” Cashman said, as Pinsky is not involved in draft operations, and teams typically don’t make major moves during that early in the season.
Pinsky was also fortunate that Cashman is a proponent of chasing one’s dreams and leaping at unique opportunities.
“Ultimately, life is too short, and we gotta live it to the max. Literally, just live every day as if it’s your last day. Don’t put things off if you have a chance to do something special,” said Cashman, who has repelled skyscrapers, swam with sharks and jumped out of a plane. “We all should be living our lives to the best of our abilities and challenging ourselves on a daily basis so there’s no regrets on the back end.”
Plus, with Pinsky fighting just 20 other contestants for “Survivor’s” $1 million grand prize, Cashman couldn’t deny him those odds.
“He would have a 1-in-21 chance of winning that, which is a hell of a lot better than when you’re playing Powerball and Mega Millions,” Cashman said.
Understanding how much this could mean to Pinsky on multiple levels, Cashman took the conversation to Steinbrenner. He signed off before Pinsky was officially cast on the show.
Pinsky, who also applied to be on Season 49, then kept the Yankees updated as he advanced through the casting process. As he got closer to the final cut, he and his superiors laid out a plan for how the front office would manage his absence.
“It was an extremely strange experience missing parts of the year,” Pinsky said.
As Pinsky navigated “Survivor’s” various challenges, he realized that working in baseball and being on the show had a lot in common. Among them: a need to collect information, build relationships, and problem solve alongside people from all walks of life.
There’s also the relentless pace of both.
“The game is always on while you’re out there. It’s really another thing that reminds me of life in a front office and life in baseball. Even when the team has an off day, it’s not really an off day, and baseball never stops,” Pinsky said. “’Survivor’ is constantly happening. It’s happening when you’re sleeping. It’s happening when you wake up. It’s happening when you take two seconds to yourself.
“It is a real mental workout, and it is not for the weak or the scared.”
Pinsky, who grew up in Manhattan and has lived in New York most of his life, said that he did not arrive in Fiji with too many practical skills that made him well-suited for “Survivor,” though.
“Not in particular,” he said when asked if he’s a big outdoorsman. “I spend more of my time in ballparks and at desks rather than building shelters and fires.”
Still, he thinks his ability to “figure things out on the fly” helped him on the show, and the talent evaluator gave himself a strong assessment without revealing how far he made it.
So did Cashman, who plans to watch Pinsky on “Survivor,” even if the Bombers’ schedule won’t let him follow in real time early on. He’s hoping that Yankees fans do, too.
“I don’t know the field, but I know the person,” Cashman said, “and I would bet on the person every day of the week. He’s extremely bright, extremely likable and process oriented. He’s taught us a lot. He’s helped elevate our game with his contributions on a year-in, year-out basis, and so I think he’s got a chance to show the world what a quality human being he is and what a quality, sophisticated contributor he can be.
“I have no doubt that he can find his way to be the last person standing, so I’m rooting for him.”

From June 1 through the August 3 deadline, the New York Yankees were hurting for offense. The club ranked 28th during that span in OPS with a .672 mark. They were 26th in runs scored with 214, an average of 3.96 per game during that 54-game period. The Yankees collectively slashed a putrid .221/.283/.389.
As a result, Brian Cashman went out and bolstered the offense. He acquired Heliot Ramos, who was brutal at the start of his tenure in New York, but has bounced back over the past three weeks. Ramos, though, was an upgrade on the margins as a platoon bat brought into mash lefties. The real get was former Washington Nationals first baseman Luis Garcia Jr.
Garcia Jr. has looked like a budding star, so this next part is tough. He joined an already crowded first base-DH rotation that includes a fringe MVP candidate in Ben Rice and a former MVP who still plays like one against lefties, Paul Goldschmidt, with a 1.006 OPS this season against southpaws.
It made sense, except for one gigantic looming development. The Yankees were expecting to get Aaron Judge back before the end of the season, who would have a much greater impact on New York's offensive output than any external addition could have by a wide margin.
That created a situation that when Judge returned after missing over three months of action, he'd immediately have to jump back in to right field. The Yankees were unable to protect his body and easy him back in at DH thanks to the logjam Cashman created, and as a result, Judge is heading back to the IL after just seven games back. Now, his status for the playoffs is in peril.
Brian Cashman's lack of trade deadline vision put Aaron Judge and the Yankees' World Series hopes at risk
First, a caveat. Judge could have wound up with a calf injury even if he wasn't playing right field. We can get into whether or not he needed more time to ramp up and was brought back too fast, but that's a discussion for another day.
The fact of the matter is that Cashman went out at the deadline and reconstructed the roster in such a way that Judge could only play right field upon his return. That was a mistake.
Now, the market wasn't exactly flush with options, but with some creativity and a willingness to be bold, Cashman could have still completed the necessary task of upgrading the offense while ensuring Judge could be protected by being inserted into the DH spot upon activation.
For example, rather than relying on George Lombard Jr. to man shortstop and provide a spark, he could have gone out and gotten an established young star at the position like Zach Neto or CJ Abrams. Neither player moved at the deadline, but for the right package, they would have. It might have cost Lombard Jr. to get it done, but as we've seen sometimes holding on to even the best prospects can end poorly.
Another lever Cashman could've pulled would've been flexing the franchise's financial might and absorbing Rafael Devers' contract. Yes, Devers just underwent season-ending core muscle surgery, but his blistering .275/.375/.611 second-half performance would have at least bridged the gap until Judge was ready, and perhaps he wouldn't have suffered the same fate had he been dealt here.
Devers has played mostly first base and DH, but while he's not a great third baseman, that's where he has the most experience, and he could've benefited from playing next to the rangy Lombard Jr. Maybe not an ideal solution, but it would've solved the logjam.
Lastly, he could have thought outside the box and beat the Dodgers offer for Tarik Skubal. This wouldn't have helped the offense, but hey, if you struggle to score, you can still win if you make it even harder for your opponent to scratch runs across. In the meantime, the coaching staff could try to figure out why the bats had been so putrid yet hit the third-most homers in MLB (76) during that otherwise horrendous 54-game stretch.
At the end of the day, Cashman did what he always does and went out and got the controllable player with projection over the established star in order to keep his prospect cost down. As a result, he created a logjam that put unnecessary risk on his three-time MVP. If Judge isn't ready in time for the start of October baseball, it will be a devastating blow to the Yankees' World Series aspirations, and it was all completely avoidable.

The New York Yankees aren't nicknamed the Bronx Bombers for no reason. For that reason, they've been well represented in the Louisville Slugger Silver Slugger Awards throughout the years. The Yankees have multiple representatives at every position except for one: shortstop.
This is in part because the award was first introduced in 1980, meaning that franchise greats and champions like Phil Rizzuto and Frank Crosetti missed the boat by a large margin. Another mitigating factor is that New York had one player dominate the position for much of the Silver Slugger era. That, of course, is Derek Jeter, who had a stranglehold on the position for the better part of two decades, taking home the award five times himself.
But while it seems like yesterday, Jeter's last big league season was in 2014. Since then, the position has looked pretty bleak. From 2015 through the present day, the Yankees have gotten a .715 OPS out of the position, which ranks 15th in the majors during that span.
That number includes the Didi Gregorius years, which included some very fine performances. Gregorius hit 97 homers in pinstripes over five seasons, while slashing .269/.313/.446. That's nothing to sneeze at, but he was never the AL's best hitter at the position during his time here.
Gregorius left following the 2019 season, and since then, things have been bleak. From 2020 onward, we have mostly been dealing with Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Anthony Volpe at short. In that time period, Yankees shortstops have produced a .668 OPS, ranking 26th in baseball.
The Yankees can't continue getting subpar offensive production out of the shortstop position
Right now, the hope for the future is George Lombard Jr. The club's top prospect got off to a hot start, but since then, he's cooled substantially. It's too early to write him off just yet, especially at just 21 years old. However, the Yankees can't afford to get into another Volpe-esque holding pattern where years go by and no material improvements are made.
That leaves the front office with an interesting conundrum. Shortstops who can hit and field don't grow on trees, and while Brian Cashman passed on a generational shortstop free-agent class to sign IKF to keep the seat warm for Volpe, he cannot afford to repeat the same lethargic approach to the position.
Ideally, Lombard Jr. snatches the job for the next 20 years with a strong finish to 2026, a postseason to remember, and a spring training that eliminates all doubt. Jeter met with the promising youngster to advise him on the responsibilities that lie ahead. Now we'll see if he took those lessons to heart.
But if we come to the conclusion of New York's 2026 campaign and haven't seen Lombard Jr. show signs that he can consistently rise to the occasion; the Yankees must be opportunistic when it comes to pursuing upgrades.
After being wrapped up in rumors at the trade deadline, it's thought that the Angels could revisit trade talks for Zach Neto in the offseason. Another possible scenario is that the Astros follow the Kyle Tucker path and trade Jeremy Peña this winter ahead of his final year of team control.
In an ideal situation, the Yankees could acquire a player like Neto or Peña while retaining Lombard Jr. to hedge their bets. Worst-case scenario: Lombard Jr. busts, and the team has a high-end veteran to man the position. Best-case scenario: they have to undertake some shuffling, but Lombard Jr. is a star, and the team is deeper and better for it.
What can't happen is the Yankees put all their eggs in the Lombard Jr. bucket, and then miss out on young stars in their prime and let the position languish for another half-decade. The time to wait and see is over, and the time to be bold is now.

PHOENIX — Los Yankees se han pasado todo el mes de septiembre intentando convertir su clasificación para la postemporada en una plantilla más clara de cara a octubre. Una de sus decisiones más difíciles de tomar ahora mismo tiene que ver con la tercera base.
Ryan McMahon llegó como un jugador que aportaba estabilidad sobre todo en defensa, pero cada vez le cuesta más ocultar su bateo. Su último bache se produjo el miércoles en el Target Field, donde se fue de 0 de 6 con cuatro strikeouts en la derrota por 5-4, en 13 entradas, ante los Minnesota Twins.
Los Yankees no dejaron de remontar. Anthony Volpe empató el partido con un doble en la novena entrada. Ali Sánchez puso a Nueva York por delante en la décima, y José Caballero sumó un fly de sacrificio en la undécima. Minnesota respondió en cada ocasión hasta que Víctor Caratini sentenció el partido con un sencillo decisivo en la 13.ª. Tommy Nance se llevó la victoria, John Schreiber la derrota y no hubo salvamento.
McMahon, que bateaba séptimo, terminó la noche con un promedio de .210/.275/.346, 10 jonrones y 34 carreras impulsadas en 118 partidos. Se ha puesto a cero 101 veces, lo que supone un porcentaje del 29,2 %, mientras que su OPS es de .621. Las estadísticas avanzadas actuales que acompañan a las críticas le sitúan en un wRC+ de 77 y un fWAR de 0,5.
Este momento hace que cada turno al bate sin resultado se note más. Los Yankees llegaban al viernes con un balance de 88-64, a cinco partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Jazz Chisholm Jr. sigue en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Volpe ha vuelto de la Triple A y ha jugado como segunda base.
La trayectoria de Volpe en las ligas menores ha ampliado las opciones de los Yankees. Durante su etapa en la Triple A, jugó como shortstop, segunda base y tercera base. Eso no significa que sea la solución definitiva para la tercera base, pero le da a Aaron Boone otra opción de alineación que tener en cuenta cuando vuelva Chisholm.
McMahon también tiene un sueldo garantizado de 16 millones de dólares para 2027. Los Yankees tienen que decidir si su defensa y su contrato siguen justificando que sea titular cuando la diferencia en ataque se ha vuelto tan grande.
McMahon entra en la zona de peligro de LeMahieu
Esa combinación ha hecho que cada vez más gente de los Yankees se plantee una pregunta más dura: si McMahon debería perder su puesto de titular, quedar fuera de la plantilla de la postemporada o, al final, ser designado para cesión.
La comparación que está cobrando fuerza es la de DJ LeMahieu, a quien los Yankees dejaron libre en julio de 2025 cuando aún le quedaban por cobrar unos 22 millones de dólares. Según FanGraphs, en su última temporada con los Yankees, LeMahieu registró un wRC+ de 94, un porcentaje de embasado de 0,338 y una tasa de strikeouts del 24,6 %.
McMahon está por debajo de todos esos indicadores ofensivos. Su porcentaje de llegada a base de 0,275 y su tasa de strikeouts del 29,2 % hacen que los Yankees obtengan menos aportación ofensiva de la que recibían de LeMahieu antes de decidir que ya no encajaba en su plantilla.
Las situaciones no son iguales. LeMahieu tenía 36 años, su papel se había reducido y Nueva York quería a Chisholm en segunda base. McMahon es más joven y sigue aportando valor en tercera base. Pero la decisión sobre LeMahieu dejó claro que el dinero garantizado no siempre protege el puesto de un veterano en la plantilla.
Boone sigue centrándose en el grupo
Los Yankees no han dicho públicamente que McMahon vaya a quedar fuera de la plantilla. Tras asegurarse el título, Boone habló de cómo el vestuario había afrontado una temporada difícil, en lugar de dar a entender que se hubiera tomado ninguna decisión sobre un veterano.
«Pero hay que reconocerles el mérito de haberse mantenido unidos. A pesar de todos los altibajos, han sido un grupo muy unido», dijo Boone.
Ese comentario no aclara cuál será el papel de McMahon en octubre. Lo que sí hace es resaltar la diferencia entre las presiones externas para que lo echen y la decisión que los Yankees hayan tomado realmente.
La defensa ya no es la respuesta definitiva
El argumento más sólido de McMahon sigue siendo su guante. La instantánea que te he pasado muestra un DRS de -1 y un Fielding Run Value de +1, mientras que la página en directo de Statcast muestra un valor defensivo global ligeramente positivo. La cifra exacta varía según la métrica y el momento de la actualización, pero la ventaja defensiva no oculta un OPS de 0,621.
Un tercera base con un OPS de 0,621 puede seguir siendo una opción válida si su defensa es de primera y el resto de la alineación está en forma. Los Yankees tienen menos margen mientras Chisholm esté de baja, y en octubre cada puesto de la alineación cobra más importancia.
Volpe no es un tercera base contrastado en las Grandes Ligas, y los Yankees no han dado a entender que tengan pensado darle esa posición. Aun así, su reciente actuación en esa posición en la Triple A le da a Boone una alternativa real. Su experiencia como campocorto hace que la objeción sobre la potencia de su brazo no sea tan sencilla, pero eso no garantiza que vaya a defender bien la tercera base en octubre.
La comparación de Okamoto hay que ponerla en contexto
Otra comparación que circula entre los aficionados de los Yankees compara a McMahon con el tercera base de Toronto, Kazuma Okamoto. Según la MLB, Okamoto tiene un promedio de bateo de 0,235, con 33 jonrones, 88 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de 0,774. Su contrato de cuatro años y 60 millones de dólares tiene un valor medio anual de 15 millones de dólares.
McMahon gana 16 millones de dólares y lleva 10 jonrones con un OPS de 0,621. A primera vista, el contraste es enorme.
No se trata de una decisión de la directiva en la que se pueda comparar a uno con otro sin más. McMahon ya tenía contrato cuando los Yankees lo ficharon en 2025, mientras que Okamoto llegó a la MLB siguiendo un camino diferente como agente libre. Aun así, la comparación salarial ayuda a entender por qué se han intensificado las críticas y por qué algunas de ellas se han extendido hasta el director general, Brian Cashman.
Octubre obliga a los Yankees a decidirse por un papel
No hay indicios confirmados de que los Yankees hayan decidido designar a McMahon para cesión o sacarlo de la plantilla de la postemporada. Sigue en activo, y la incertidumbre sobre la fecha de regreso de Chisholm hace que la situación en el cuadro siga siendo incierta.
Pero la cuestión ya no es si McMahon está pasando por una mala racha. Es cuánto tiempo de juego pueden permitirse los Yankees darle a un bateador con un wRC+ de 77 cuando empiece octubre.
Nueva York comienza este viernes una serie de tres partidos en el Chase Field contra Arizona. McMahon tiene tiempo para cambiar el rumbo, pero los Yankees ahora tienen menos margen de maniobra y más alternativas en el cuadro que hace un mes.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

On the offensive front, the New York Yankees have a lot to worry about. Pitching-wise, things are okay — more than okay, actually.
Despite a lackluster trade deadline in which general manager Brian Cashman failed to add any relievers, the team bolstered its pitching depth in the weeks that followed. They lucked out by adding John Schreiber, which was essentially a salary dump for the Kansas City Royals, and Clarke Schmidt coming off the IL is another positive.
The Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon was an ugly one they needed, and Minnesota's walk-off left a bad taste, while Aaron Judge had another injury scare. But it was another stellar day for the pen, outside of David Bednar letting up two leads in extras. Schmidt is one reason to look forward to what the pen could be in October, and even if he has a little more rust to knock off, there are a few things to be excited about.
Giving length
Schmidt isn't built up, but he should be good to give a little more than an inning at a time as a reliever. While he only pitched 2/3 innings in his return to the mound, it's clear the Yankees are building Schmidt up to go multiple innings. In three of his five rehab starts, he pitched more than one inning. In two of them, he pitched two innings.
Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick have clearly been overworked. Somebody like Schmidt lightens their load, and soon another starter, Ryan Weathers, will join the bullpen.
More strikeout stuff in the bullpen
The Yankees have desperately needed strikeout stuff, especially in the middle innings. The Yankees have guys who can generate whiffs in Bednar, Blackburn, and Headrick, but that's missing if a starter comes out early. Schmidt gives them that. He struck out two batters in his debut, and despite allowing two hits, he navigated through it because of the whiffs.
Schmidt also showed strikeout stuff in his rehab start. He struck out 11 batters in seven innings. He hasn't had a full season since 2023, but in 2024 and 2025 combined, the veteran hurler had a 9.11 K/9. That should play in October.
No more sweeper?
The sweeper was Schmidt's second-most-used pitch in 2024. It was his third-most-used pitch in 2023. Against the Minnesota Twins, he didn't throw it once. It could be a pitch he's throwing away.
It would be a surprise if he did that, though. Batters hit .210 off it and struck out 33.8% of the time against it in 2024. In 2025, they hit .125 off the sweeper. They struck out 35.8% of the time against it. It's something to look to in future outings.
Potential trade bait
You can never have too much pitching, and if there is one thing the 2026 Yankees understand full well, it's that pitching depth is paramount. It's how they navigated the season.
That said, Schmidt has one year left after this season. The Yankees may want to sell high on him if they don't plan on bringing him back. The rotation should be full again next year, and if they need pitching depth, they have Ryan Weathers and Will Warren.
This season could be a showcase of sorts for Schmidt. The veteran showing he can finish out the season could be a selling point in the winter.
Chances are, Schmidt won't be able to start next year anyway, and if he does, he won't have a full workload since he needs to build back up. The last time he pitched more than 150 innings was in 2023. That said, the Yankees could use this as an opportunity to deal an oft-injured pitcher and fill another area of need.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe is four games into his new role as a big-league second baseman after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Volpe hasn't committed an error yet, and while the sample is tiny, the eye test feels so right. Volpe just looks comfortable out there.
His Jeter-esque jump throw on Sunday (from second base, but still!) was such a rewarding watch for Yankees fans who have experienced the dreadful lows of Volpe's up-and-down season and career. It looked and felt so much more iconic than it was.
It didn't take long for Anthony Volpe to learn second base for the Yankees
Volpe looking smooth at second is a bittersweet reality for Yankees fans, especially those with a quick trigger to criticize the team's development and roster decisions. On one hand, New York's decision to send Volpe down to the minors and learn second base this season has ... worked! On the other hand, this exact plan should have been put into motion a long time ago.
It's kind of like turning in your book report a month late in middle school. The teacher is like, "Well, thanks ... but I just remembered again that you never handed this in." You might've been better off just taking the zero and acing the next one.
If Volpe keeps acing second base — and sustains this level of defense into 2027 and beyond alongside George Lombard Jr. — the Yankees will have salvaged Volpe's career and somewhat made up for their entire mishandling of his development.
Then again, should the Yankees really get any credit for salvaging anything here, especially since it was the organization itself that contributed to this mess? Even now, it took an injury to Chisholm (not his horrid season and Volpe's red-hot bat in the minors) to give Volpe another opportunity. This decision was made for the Yankees, not by them. And it came way, way too late. On second thought, they don't get any credit here.
Anthony Volpe as a second-base solution should have been obvious to the Yankees years ago
Any player evaluator of worth should have been able to look at Volpe and surmise that a move from shortstop to second base made sense. Volpe won a Gold Glove as a rookie shortstop in 2023, but his range, arm, and consistency declined after that. Isn't that pretty much the precise recipe for a move from short to second, if you had to literally write the script?
The Yankees' problem with Volpe over the years, as has been acknowledged ad nauseam, is that they made "New York Yankees starting shortstop" Volpe's identity (rather than his job) and hugged that identity too tightly. It became a stranglehold that suffocated Volpe and had Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman at their most delusional in interviews, which is saying a lot.
The funny thing is that Volpe's never been against changing positions. He said unironically that he'd play catcher. It was Boone and Cashman who were stubborn, and they never actually lessened their grip on this situation. George Lombard Jr. undid that grip for them, and then Chisholm went down.
To the non-Yankee fan, the Yankees might look smart for putting Volpe at second base. But for the die-hards, this decision — and Volpe's good performance at second so far — hurts as much as it excites. At least for now.

BRONX, N.Y. — Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada y siguen a 3 1/2 partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Pero una de las decisiones más importantes que ha tomado la organización este mes de septiembre no tiene nada que ver con la alineación de Aaron Boone ni con los planes de pitcheo para octubre.
Esto ha dado lugar a seis despidos en lo que va de septiembre.
Todo esto está pasando a miles de millas del Yankee Stadium, en la República Dominicana, Venezuela y otros mercados donde se descubre a los futuros Yankees años antes de que la mayoría de los aficionados sepan siquiera sus nombres.
De esa cantera salieron Robinson Canó, Alfonso Soriano, Gary Sánchez e Iván Nova. Los Yankees siguieron invirtiendo ahí a medida que cambiaban las normas sobre bonificaciones, la tecnología y los métodos de evaluación de jugadores amateurs.
La presión sobre esa área lleva meses aumentando. Donny Rowland, director de ojeadores internacionales desde hacía mucho tiempo, no renovó su contrato cuando este expiró en noviembre. Los Yankees ascendieron entonces a Mario Garza, que llevaba 16 años en la organización y tenía experiencia en el desarrollo de jugadores, las operaciones en Latinoamérica y el desarrollo del béisbol, para que se encargara de los ojeadores internacionales en enero.
La transición tuvo un coste inmediato. Wandy Asigen, uno de los mejores jugadores de la promoción internacional de 2026, se echó atrás en el acuerdo que tenía previsto con los Yankees tras la marcha de Rowland y fichó por los Mets por 3,9 millones de dólares. Nueva York también empezó el periodo de fichajes con un fondo de 5,44 millones de dólares, el más bajo de la MLB (empatado con otro equipo) tras perder un millón de dólares por fichar a Max Fried.
Cuando Garza se hizo cargo, Brian Cashman describió algo que iba más allá de un simple cambio de personal.
«Es un gran evaluador de talento», dijo Cashman. «Conoce nuestros sistemas. Ya sabe todo el personal que queremos tener. Quieres evaluación, quieres que todo esté conectado con la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos. Eso le dará ventaja a la hora de relanzar ese departamento y seguir adelante».
Esas declaraciones públicas cobran ahora importancia porque dejaron claro, meses antes de septiembre, que Nueva York veía el departamento como algo que había que reconstruir, en lugar de simplemente mantener.
El relanzamiento se ha convertido en una reestructuración más amplia de los Yankees
Ese relanzamiento se ha acelerado.
Cinco empleados del departamento de ojeadores internacionales de los Yankees no han sido renovados en lo que el periodista Francys Romero ha descrito como una «primera oleada». Se trata de los ojeadores de la zona de la República Dominicana José Sabino y Arturo Peña Jr., el ojeador de la zona de Santo Domingo Moisés Brito, el asistente de vídeo Miguel Mojica y el supervisor de Venezuela José Gavidia.
Romero describió los cambios como parte de un plan más amplio.
«Los Yankees tienen previsto reestructurar su departamento de ojeadores internacionales y, según fuentes del sector, ya han despedido a cinco personas en los últimos días. Entre los ojeadores que no seguirán están José Sabino y Arturo Peña Jr. (ojeador de la zona de Cibao, República Dominicana), Moisés Brito (ojeador de la zona de Santo Domingo), Miguel Mojica (asistente de vídeo) y José Gavidia (supervisor de Venezuela)».
Estas medidas se produjeron tras la salida del veterano ojeador Víctor Mata, cuya trayectoria en los Yankees se prolongó durante más de tres décadas. Mata ayudó a evaluar o fichar a Canó, Sánchez, Soriano, Nova y Zoilo Almonte.
La naturaleza exacta de la salida de Mata sigue siendo objeto de debate. Romero informó de que los Yankees lo dejaron marchar. El periodista Mike Rodríguez ofreció una versión diferente, afirmando que Mata se retiró y recibió las prestaciones asociadas a su larga trayectoria en el equipo. Los Yankees no han dado públicamente una explicación detallada.
La cronología apunta a un reinicio planificado
La racha es más larga que los movimientos de esta semana.
A Rowland no le renovaron el contrato en noviembre. Garza fue nombrado en enero y Cashman utilizó públicamente la palabra «relanzamiento». Los Yankees funcionaron entonces toda la temporada bajo un nuevo liderazgo antes de la marcha de Mata y los cinco cambios adicionales en la plantilla que se produjeron en septiembre.
Esto apunta más bien a un reajuste estructural que a una reacción ante un solo prospecto o una sola promoción de fichajes.
Había motivos para replantearse los resultados. Un análisis de FanGraphs sobre el sistema de cantera de los Yankees, publicado en marzo, señalaba que el club solía destinar una gran parte de su fondo de bonificaciones internacionales a uno o dos jugadores caros y que demasiadas de esas apuestas millonarias no habían dado los frutos esperados.
En ese mismo informe se decía que el sistema necesitaba más talento entre los jugadores de campo tras las últimas salidas por graduación. Eso no aclara por qué se despidió a ningún ojeador, pero ayuda a entender por qué los Yankees se replantearían cómo identifican, valoran y forman a los jugadores internacionales.
La marcha de Asigen hizo que el tema cobrara más relevancia. Este campocorto de 16 años estaba considerado uno de los mejores jugadores de su generación y se esperaba que firmara con los Yankees, pero cambió de planes tras la salida de Rowland.
Ahora los comentarios que hizo Cashman en enero parecen más importantes
La pista más clara sobre qué hay detrás de la reorganización de los Yankees podría haber llegado ocho meses antes de los últimos cambios.
La descripción que hizo Cashman de Garza hacía hincapié en la colaboración entre la evaluación, la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos. El currículum de Garza une todas esas áreas. Antes de este puesto, fue director de desarrollo de béisbol en 2024 y 2025, y anteriormente trabajó en operaciones en Latinoamérica y en el desarrollo de jugadores internacionales.
Esto hace que los cambios parezcan menos un rechazo al ojeo tradicional y más un intento de cambiar cómo circula la información de ojeo por la organización.
El ojeo internacional sigue dependiendo de las relaciones, la evaluación presencial y el conocimiento local. La carrera de Mata puso de manifiesto ese valor. Pero ahora los Yankees están colocando al frente del departamento a un líder con experiencia reciente en desarrollo y sistemas.
La apuesta es importante. Nueva York está dejando atrás a miembros del equipo con profundas raíces en Latinoamérica, al tiempo que pide a un nuevo grupo que mantenga esas relaciones y modernice la evaluación al mismo tiempo.
El veredicto tardará años en salir
No hay resultados inmediatos que reflejen una reforma en el sistema de ojeadores internacionales.
Un cambio en la alineación se puede valorar esa misma noche. Pero una decisión que afecte a un joven promesa de 16 años puede que no dé frutos en las Grandes Ligas hasta dentro de cinco o seis años.
Eso es lo que hace que el momento sea tan significativo. Los Yankees tienen un balance de 88-63, se han asegurado un puesto en octubre y ocupan la primera plaza de comodín de la Liga Americana. Sin embargo, estos cambios están pensados para las plantillas mucho más allá de la actual carrera por los playoffs.
La cronología que se conoce está clara: Rowland se va, ascienden a Garza, se pierde a uno de los mejores fichajes, Mata se marcha y no se renueva a otros cinco miembros del personal internacional. Lo que los Yankees no han dicho públicamente es si habrá más cambios.
Por ahora, las declaraciones de Cashman en enero son las que ofrecen una explicación más clara. Los Yankees querían relanzar el departamento y vincular más estrechamente el trabajo de ojeadores con la ciencia del rendimiento y el análisis de datos.
Ocho meses después, ese relanzamiento está cambiando el perfil de las personas que decidirán qué jóvenes jugadores entrarán próximamente en el sistema de los Yankees.

The New York Yankees added Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos ahead of the trade deadline, but the big concern, the bullpen, was an area where Brian Cashman walked away empty-handed. In the following weeks, the front office made some moves through the waiver wire, and adding John Schreiber has somewhat remedied their deadline whiff.
This season, Schreiber has a 3.20 ERA in 56.1 IP. It's as low as it is because the veteran reliever has posted zeroes in the run column in every outing that Aaron Boone has turned to him. When the Kansas City Royals cut him loose — most likely for monetary reasons — he was sitting on a 3.65 ERA, and his seven-inning scoreless streak in pinstripes has brought that to where Schreiber has been for most of his career.
One thing about Schreiber is that while he isn't getting the strikeouts he once did, he's been able to give length when needed, too. In three of the six appearances, Schreiber has pitched 1.1 innings. That ability matters as much as his dependability, because the bullpen needed a few more arms to carry the load for Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick — two guys who carried the Yankees through a year-long medley of close games.
His most recent outing in which he did this was the first game against the Minnesota Twins on Monday night. In the bottom of the eighth, Tim Hill gave up a home run to Josh Bell, Emmanuel Rodriguez reached on an error, and Victor Caratini reached base after he was hit by a pitch. Schreiber was then tasked with getting four outs for Boone. He started by shutting the door on Minnesota's budding rally.
In the ninth, after walking Luke Keaschell, Schreiber induced a double play. That inning got a little dicey, though, after a walk and another error, but Schreiber danced around the base runners without David Bednar needing to come in.
A lucky add for the Yankees
While Schreiber has been fantastic in New York, it's hard to credit his success to Matt Blake magic. Schreiber has always been one of baseball's more dependable relievers, and his 3.20 ERA is slightly lower than his career 3.57 across Detroit, Boston, and Kansas City.
Schreiber is actually the type of pitcher the Yankees needed to acquire at the deadline. There was a lot of talk about a blockbuster Mason Miller deal, but what this team needed most was a few veteran arms who can be dependable in higher-leverage spots, so Boone isn't forced to go to Hendrick and Blackburn. Schreiber has been exactly that, and the Yankees are lucky the Royals wanted to save a few dollars with him.
